articles.body_html:
🚪 Why the WP REST API Deserves Your Attention

Every WordPress site already ships with a front door for data. Open yourdomain.com/wp-json/ and you'll see a big JSON map of everything the site can do. That's the WordPress REST API.

It lets anything that speaks HTTP talk to WordPress: a React app, a mobile app, a Zapier flow, or another website. No admin screens, no page reloads. Just JSON in, JSON out.

In this article we'll go from "what is this thing?" to a complete, secure CRUD API for a custom Bookshelf, step by step.

By the end you'll know how to:

  • Register your own routes
  • Use GET, POST, PUT, PATCH and DELETE
  • Share one URL across several HTTP methods (the part that confuses almost everyone!)
  • Validate, sanitize and protect every request

Let's go. 🚀

🧠 Part 1: The WP REST API in Plain English

Think of the REST API as a restaurant:

  • Namespace → the restaurant name (bookshelf/v1)
  • Route → the menu item (/books)
  • Method → what you want to do with it (order, change, cancel)
  • Callback → the kitchen that does the work
  • Permission callback → the bouncer at the door 🕴️

A full URL looks like this:

https://example.com/wp-json/bookshelf/v1/books/42
                    └─ base ─┘└namespace┘└route┘└id┘

WordPress already gives you built-in endpoints under the wp/v2 namespace:

# Latest 5 posts
curl "https://example.com/wp-json/wp/v2/posts?per_page=5"

Those are great for posts, pages and users. But the moment you have your own data (books, bookings, tickets, whatever), you'll want custom routes.

🔤 HTTP methods at a glance

Method Typical meaning WP constant
GET Read data WP_REST_Server::READABLE
POST Create data WP_REST_Server::CREATABLE
PUT / PATCH Update data WP_REST_Server::EDITABLE (it also includes POST)
DELETE Remove data WP_REST_Server::DELETABLE
ALLMETHODS Everything above WP_REST_Server::ALLMETHODS

Two methods you didn't ask about but should know:

  • PATCH → a partial update ("only change the rating").
  • OPTIONS → WordPress answers automatically with your route's schema and allowed methods. You get it for free. 🎁

🧩 The four pieces of every endpoint

When you register a route, each handler has these keys:

Key What it does
methods Which HTTP verbs this handler accepts
callback The function that does the work
permission_callback Who is allowed in (required, WordPress warns you if it's missing)
args The parameters, with type, required, default, enum, minimum, maximum, sanitize_callback, validate_callback

Your callback receives a WP_REST_Request and should return a WP_REST_Response (or a WP_Error when something goes wrong).

🛠️ Part 2: Creating Your First Custom Route

Routes are registered on the rest_api_init hook. Here's the smallest useful example:

add_action( 'rest_api_init', function () {
    register_rest_route(
        'bookshelf/v1',
        '/ping',
        array(
            'methods'             => WP_REST_Server::READABLE,
            'callback'            => function () {
                return rest_ensure_response( array( 'message' => 'pong' ) );
            },
            'permission_callback' => '__return_true', // Public on purpose.
        )
    );
} );

Visit /wp-json/bookshelf/v1/ping and you'll get {"message":"pong"}. 🎉

🔗 Dynamic routes with URL parameters

Need an ID in the URL? Use a regex capture group:

register_rest_route(
    'bookshelf/v1',
    '/books/(?P<id>\d+)',
    array( /* handlers go here */ )
);

Inside the callback, read it with $request->get_param( 'id' ). The \d+ also means /books/abc never reaches your code, so WordPress returns a 404 for you.

🏗️ A clean OOP structure

Since we're building a real API, let's keep it tidy. One class per job:

bookshelf/
├── bookshelf.php               ← Plugin bootstrap
└── includes/
    ├── class-plugin.php        ← Wires everything up
    ├── class-book-post-type.php ← Registers the "book" post type
    └── class-books-controller.php ← All REST logic lives here

For storage we'll use a private custom post type called book. This way we get trash, revisions and capabilities for free:

<?php
/**
 * Registers the Book post type.
 *
 * @package Bookshelf
 */

namespace Bookshelf;

defined( 'ABSPATH' ) || exit;

/**
 * Class Book_Post_Type
 */
class Book_Post_Type {

    /**
     * Hook into WordPress.
     *
     * @return void
     */
    public function register_hooks(): void {
        add_action( 'init', array( $this, 'register' ) );
    }

    /**
     * Register the post type (hidden from the default REST output).
     *
     * @return void
     */
    public function register(): void {
        register_post_type(
            'book',
            array(
                'label'        => __( 'Books', 'bookshelf' ),
                'public'       => false,
                'show_ui'      => true,
                'show_in_rest' => false, // We expose it with our own API.
                'supports'     => array( 'title' ),
            )
        );
    }
}

🔀 Part 3: Same Route, Different Methods

Here's the question I hear the most:

"If /books is used for both listing and creating, how does WordPress know which function to run?"

It looks at the HTTP method. The route is the address. The method is the intent. 📬

The trick is to pass an array of handlers to a single register_rest_route() call. Each handler declares its own methods, callback, permissions and args:

register_rest_route(
    'bookshelf/v1',
    '/books',
    array(
        // Handler 1: GET /books → list books.
        array(
            'methods'             => WP_REST_Server::READABLE,
            'callback'            => array( $this, 'get_items' ),
            'permission_callback' => '__return_true',
            'args'                => $this->get_collection_args(),
        ),
        // Handler 2: POST /books → create a book.
        array(
            'methods'             => WP_REST_Server::CREATABLE,
            'callback'            => array( $this, 'create_item' ),
            'permission_callback' => array( $this, 'can_create' ),
            'args'                => $this->get_write_args( true ),
        ),
    )
);

Same URL, two different jobs, two different bouncers. Notice that listing is public while creating needs a capability.

🔍 What WordPress does on each request

  1. Matches the URL against every registered route (the regex).
  2. Finds the handler whose methods contains the request's method.
  3. Runs the permission_callback (fail → 401 or 403).
  4. Validates and sanitizes args (fail → 400).
  5. Finally runs your callback. ✅

⚠️ Gotchas worth remembering

  • Method not registered? If you send DELETE /books and no handler accepts it, you get a 404 rest_no_route. WordPress treats "route + method" as the unit.
  • Don't mix up the args. Each handler has its own args. Creating a book needs a required title, but listing a book needs optional page and per_page.
  • EDITABLE includes POST. If you use WP_REST_Server::EDITABLE on /books/{id}, then POST /books/5 will also update. It's handy, but it can surprise you. In this article I'll list PUT and PATCH explicitly.
  • One call is cleaner. Calling register_rest_route() twice for the same route merges the handlers, but keeping them together in one call makes the code much easier to read.

📚 Part 4: The Complete Bookshelf API

Here's the endpoint map we're building. Keep this table handy, we'll go through it top to bottom:

Method Endpoint Purpose
POST /wp-json/bookshelf/v1/books Create a book
GET /wp-json/bookshelf/v1/books List books with pagination
GET /wp-json/bookshelf/v1/books/{id} Retrieve one book
PUT / PATCH /wp-json/bookshelf/v1/books/{id} Update a book
DELETE /wp-json/bookshelf/v1/books/{id} Delete a book

🧱 The controller skeleton

All five handlers live in one class. First, the registration and the shared helpers:

<?php
/**
 * Books REST controller.
 *
 * @package Bookshelf
 */

namespace Bookshelf;

use WP_Error;
use WP_Post;
use WP_Query;
use WP_REST_Request;
use WP_REST_Response;
use WP_REST_Server;

defined( 'ABSPATH' ) || exit;

/**
 * Class Books_Controller
 */
class Books_Controller {

    const REST_NAMESPACE = 'bookshelf/v1';

    /**
     * Hook into WordPress.
     *
     * @return void
     */
    public function register_hooks(): void {
        add_action( 'rest_api_init', array( $this, 'register_routes' ) );
    }

    /**
     * Register the collection and single-item routes.
     *
     * @return void
     */
    public function register_routes(): void {
        // Collection route: /books.
        register_rest_route(
            self::REST_NAMESPACE,
            '/books',
            array(
                array(
                    'methods'             => WP_REST_Server::READABLE,
                    'callback'            => array( $this, 'get_items' ),
                    'permission_callback' => '__return_true',
                    'args'                => $this->get_collection_args(),
                ),
                array(
                    'methods'             => WP_REST_Server::CREATABLE,
                    'callback'            => array( $this, 'create_item' ),
                    'permission_callback' => array( $this, 'can_create' ),
                    'args'                => $this->get_write_args( true ),
                ),
            )
        );

        // Single-item route: /books/{id}.
        register_rest_route(
            self::REST_NAMESPACE,
            '/books/(?P<id>\d+)',
            array(
                array(
                    'methods'             => WP_REST_Server::READABLE,
                    'callback'            => array( $this, 'get_item' ),
                    'permission_callback' => '__return_true',
                ),
                array(
                    'methods'             => array( 'PUT', 'PATCH' ),
                    'callback'            => array( $this, 'update_item' ),
                    'permission_callback' => array( $this, 'can_modify' ),
                    'args'                => $this->get_write_args( false ),
                ),
                array(
                    'methods'             => WP_REST_Server::DELETABLE,
                    'callback'            => array( $this, 'delete_item' ),
                    'permission_callback' => array( $this, 'can_modify' ),
                    'args'                => array(
                        'force' => array(
                            'type'    => 'boolean',
                            'default' => false,
                        ),
                    ),
                ),
            )
        );
    }

    /**
     * Permission: can the current user create books?
     *
     * @return bool
     */
    public function can_create(): bool {
        return current_user_can( 'edit_posts' );
    }

    /**
     * Permission: can the current user edit or delete this specific book?
     *
     * @param WP_REST_Request $request Request object.
     * @return bool
     */
    public function can_modify( WP_REST_Request $request ): bool {
        return current_user_can( 'edit_post', absint( $request['id'] ) );
    }

And the argument definitions. This is where validation and sanitization happen before your callback even runs:

    /**
     * Args for the list endpoint.
     *
     * @return array
     */
    private function get_collection_args(): array {
        return array(
            'page'     => array(
                'type'              => 'integer',
                'default'           => 1,
                'minimum'           => 1,
                'sanitize_callback' => 'absint',
            ),
            'per_page' => array(
                'type'              => 'integer',
                'default'           => 10,
                'minimum'           => 1,
                'maximum'           => 50,
                'sanitize_callback' => 'absint',
            ),
            'search'   => array(
                'type'              => 'string',
                'sanitize_callback' => 'sanitize_text_field',
            ),
        );
    }

    /**
     * Args for create and update.
     *
     * @param bool $is_create Title is required only when creating.
     * @return array
     */
    private function get_write_args( bool $is_create ): array {
        return array(
            'title'  => array(
                'type'              => 'string',
                'required'          => $is_create,
                'minLength'         => 1,
                'sanitize_callback' => 'sanitize_text_field',
            ),
            'author' => array(
                'type'              => 'string',
                'sanitize_callback' => 'sanitize_text_field',
            ),
            'rating' => array(
                'type'              => 'integer',
                'minimum'           => 1,
                'maximum'           => 5,
                'sanitize_callback' => 'absint',
            ),
            'status' => array(
                'type' => 'string',
                'enum' => array( 'publish', 'draft' ),
            ),
        );
    }

Now the fun part. Each method gets its own mini-section: the code, a curl call, and the response.

💡 Testing tip: for write requests, create an Application Password (Users → Profile) and send it with curl -u "username:app-password". If you call the API from inside the browser, send the X-WP-Nonce header instead.

1️⃣ POST: Create a Book 

    /**
     * POST /books
     *
     * @param WP_REST_Request $request Request object.
     * @return WP_REST_Response|WP_Error
     */
    public function create_item( WP_REST_Request $request ) {
        $post_id = wp_insert_post(
            wp_slash(
                array(
                    'post_type'   => 'book',
                    'post_title'  => $request['title'],
                    'post_status' => $request['status'] ?? 'publish',
                    'meta_input'  => array(
                        '_bookshelf_author' => $request['author'] ?? '',
                        '_bookshelf_rating' => $request['rating'] ?? 0,
                    ),
                )
            ),
            true
        );

        if ( is_wp_error( $post_id ) ) {
            return $post_id;
        }

        $response = new WP_REST_Response( $this->prepare_item( get_post( $post_id ) ), 201 );
        $response->header( 'Location', rest_url( self::REST_NAMESPACE . '/books/' . $post_id ) );

        return $response;
    }

Notice the 201 Created status and the Location header. It's the polite REST way to say "here's where your new thing lives."

Request

curl -X POST "https://example.com/wp-json/bookshelf/v1/books" \
  -u "kushang:xxxx xxxx xxxx xxxx" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"title":"Atomic Habits","author":"James Clear","rating":5}'

Response (201)

{
  "id": 42,
  "title": "Atomic Habits",
  "author": "James Clear",
  "rating": 5,
  "status": "publish",
  "link": "https://example.com/wp-json/bookshelf/v1/books/42"
}

Forget the title? You'll automatically get a 400 with rest_missing_callback_param. You didn't write a single if for that. 😎

2️⃣ GET: List Books (with Pagination) 

    /**
     * GET /books
     *
     * @param WP_REST_Request $request Request object.
     * @return WP_REST_Response
     */
    public function get_items( WP_REST_Request $request ): WP_REST_Response {
        $query = new WP_Query(
            array(
                'post_type'      => 'book',
                'post_status'    => 'publish',
                'paged'          => $request['page'],
                'posts_per_page' => $request['per_page'],
                's'              => $request['search'] ?? '',
            )
        );

        $items = array_map( array( $this, 'prepare_item' ), $query->posts );

        $response = new WP_REST_Response( $items, 200 );
        $response->header( 'X-WP-Total', (int) $query->found_posts );
        $response->header( 'X-WP-TotalPages', (int) $query->max_num_pages );

        return $response;
    }

Pagination info goes in the headers, just like core endpoints do. Your JSON body stays a clean array.

Request

curl "https://example.com/wp-json/bookshelf/v1/books?page=1&per_page=2&search=habits"

Response (200, headers: X-WP-Total: 1, X-WP-TotalPages: 1)

[
  {
    "id": 42,
    "title": "Atomic Habits",
    "author": "James Clear",
    "rating": 5,
    "status": "publish",
    "link": "https://example.com/wp-json/bookshelf/v1/books/42"
  }
]

Try per_page=500 and you'll get a 400 back, thanks to maximum => 50. Always cap your list endpoints! 🛡️

3️⃣ GET: Retrieve One Book

We need a small helper that finds the book or returns a proper 404:

    /**
     * Fetch a book or return a 404 error.
     *
     * @param int $id Book ID.
     * @return WP_Post|WP_Error
     */
    private function get_book( int $id ) {
        $post = get_post( $id );

        if ( ! $post instanceof WP_Post || 'book' !== $post->post_type ) {
            return new WP_Error(
                'bookshelf_not_found',
                __( 'Book not found.', 'bookshelf' ),
                array( 'status' => 404 )
            );
        }

        return $post;
    }

    /**
     * GET /books/{id}
     *
     * @param WP_REST_Request $request Request object.
     * @return WP_REST_Response|WP_Error
     */
    public function get_item( WP_REST_Request $request ) {
        $book = $this->get_book( absint( $request['id'] ) );

        if ( is_wp_error( $book ) ) {
            return $book;
        }

        return new WP_REST_Response( $this->prepare_item( $book ), 200 );
    }

Request

curl "https://example.com/wp-json/bookshelf/v1/books/42"

Response (200) → the same single book object you saw above.

Missing book → 404:

{
  "code": "bookshelf_not_found",
  "message": "Book not found.",
  "data": { "status": 404 }
}

4️⃣ PUT / PATCH: Update a Book 

    /**
     * PUT|PATCH /books/{id}
     *
     * Only the fields that were sent get updated.
     *
     * @param WP_REST_Request $request Request object.
     * @return WP_REST_Response|WP_Error
     */
    public function update_item( WP_REST_Request $request ) {
        $book = $this->get_book( absint( $request['id'] ) );

        if ( is_wp_error( $book ) ) {
            return $book;
        }

        $update = array( 'ID' => $book->ID );

        if ( $request->has_param( 'title' ) ) {
            $update['post_title'] = $request['title'];
        }

        if ( $request->has_param( 'status' ) ) {
            $update['post_status'] = $request['status'];
        }

        $result = wp_update_post( wp_slash( $update ), true );

        if ( is_wp_error( $result ) ) {
            return $result;
        }

        if ( $request->has_param( 'author' ) ) {
            update_post_meta( $book->ID, '_bookshelf_author', $request['author'] );
        }

        if ( $request->has_param( 'rating' ) ) {
            update_post_meta( $book->ID, '_bookshelf_rating', $request['rating'] );
        }

        return new WP_REST_Response( $this->prepare_item( get_post( $book->ID ) ), 200 );
    }

🧠 PUT vs PATCH: by the book, PUT replaces the whole resource and PATCH changes a few fields. WordPress core is relaxed here: both are treated as "update what I sent". I'm following core's habit, since it's friendlier for clients.

Request

curl -X PATCH "https://example.com/wp-json/bookshelf/v1/books/42" \
  -u "kushang:xxxx xxxx xxxx xxxx" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"rating":4}'

Response (200)

{
  "id": 42,
  "title": "Atomic Habits",
  "author": "James Clear",
  "rating": 4,
  "status": "publish",
  "link": "https://example.com/wp-json/bookshelf/v1/books/42"
}

5️⃣ DELETE: Remove a Book 

    /**
     * DELETE /books/{id}
     *
     * Moves to trash by default. Pass force=true to delete permanently.
     *
     * @param WP_REST_Request $request Request object.
     * @return WP_REST_Response|WP_Error
     */
    public function delete_item( WP_REST_Request $request ) {
        $book = $this->get_book( absint( $request['id'] ) );

        if ( is_wp_error( $book ) ) {
            return $book;
        }

        $previous = $this->prepare_item( $book );
        $deleted  = wp_delete_post( $book->ID, (bool) $request['force'] );

        if ( ! $deleted ) {
            return new WP_Error(
                'bookshelf_delete_failed',
                __( 'The book could not be deleted.', 'bookshelf' ),
                array( 'status' => 500 )
            );
        }

        return new WP_REST_Response(
            array(
                'deleted'  => (bool) $request['force'],
                'previous' => $previous,
            ),
            200
        );
    }

Request

curl -X DELETE "https://example.com/wp-json/bookshelf/v1/books/42?force=true" \
  -u "kushang:xxxx xxxx xxxx xxxx"

Response (200)

{
  "deleted": true,
  "previous": { "id": 42, "title": "Atomic Habits", "...": "..." }
}

🎁 The Shared Formatter

One last helper so every endpoint returns the same shape. This is where we also escape the output we send out:

    /**
     * Turn a book post into a clean API array.
     *
     * @param WP_Post $post Book post.
     * @return array
     */
    private function prepare_item( WP_Post $post ): array {
        return array(
            'id'     => $post->ID,
            'title'  => $post->post_title,
            'author' => (string) get_post_meta( $post->ID, '_bookshelf_author', true ),
            'rating' => (int) get_post_meta( $post->ID, '_bookshelf_rating', true ),
            'status' => $post->post_status,
            'link'   => esc_url_raw( rest_url( self::REST_NAMESPACE . '/books/' . $post->ID ) ),
        );
    }
}

A quick note on escaping: JSON isn't HTML, so running esc_html() on API values would give clients double-encoded text like &. The rule of thumb is sanitize on the way in, escape at the place you render. Use esc_url_raw() for URLs, and let your front-end escape titles when it prints them.

🔐 Security Checklist (Pin This One)

  • ✅ Always set permission_callback. Use __return_true only for data that's truly public, and say so in a comment.
  • ✅ Validate with type, enum, minimum, maximum.
  • ✅ Sanitize with sanitize_callback before saving.
  • ✅ Check capabilities per item (edit_post) and not only globally.
  • ✅ Cap per_page.
  • ✅ Return a WP_Error with a proper status code and never die() or echo.
  • ✅ Use wp_slash() when passing REST data to wp_insert_post() and wp_update_post().

🏁 Final Verdict

The WP REST API looks big at first, but once you see the pattern it's actually tiny:

One namespace → routes → an array of handlers → each handler = methods + callback + permissions + args.

The thing to take with you is Part 3. A route is just an address, and the HTTP method decides which handler answers. Once that clicks, GET /books and POST /books living side by side stops feeling like magic.

A few honest opinions after building this:

  • 🧱 Use a controller class. A pile of closures works for demos, but a class keeps your routes testable and readable.
  • 🛡️ Let args do the heavy lifting. Declarative validation means fewer if blocks and fewer bugs.
  • 🔑 Treat permissions as a feature, not an afterthought. Most REST API security issues come from a lazy permission_callback.
  • 📦 Version your namespace (/v1). Your future self will thank you when /v2 arrives.

Now it's your turn: take the Bookshelf, swap books for whatever your project needs (tasks, events, orders), and ship something. Got questions or a cooler example? Drop them in the comments, I read every one! 💬

articles.title: slopsieve: a diff linter for the AI slop era
articles.description: cURL scrapped its bug bounty after getting buried in AI slop. Godot is drowning in slop PRs. GitHub...
articles.body_html:
cURL scrapped its bug bounty after getting buried in AI slop. Godot is drowning in slop PRs. GitHub floated a PR kill switch. the maintainers' complaint is consistent: the code looks fine until you read it.

so i built slopsieve, a zero-dep node CLI that scores a diff or PR for the 12 signals a tired reviewer checks at 1am:

$ npx slopsieve fixtures/slop.patch

SLOP SCORE: 100/100 - ALARM
4 files · +37 -8 lines

FLAGS
  [30] test weakening        tests/cart.test.js:24 it.skip(...)
  [25] debug leftovers       src/cart.js:25 console.log("checking qty", qty)
  [20] empty catch/except    src/utils.js:12 } catch (e) {}
  [20] trivial dependency    package.json:17 adds 'is-odd'
  [15] commented-out code    3 commented-out lines
  [10] narration comments    6 narration comments
  [10] dead exports          'isQuantityOdd' referenced nowhere in this diff
  [ 5] vague util sprawl     src/utils.js created

what it does: parses the unified diff, runs 12 weighted checks (it.skip, assertions removed, console.log/debugger, catch-all deps, exports nothing references, "this function..." comments), prints file and line for every flag. --fail-at makes it a CI gate, --json feeds tooling.

the bug that embarrassed me: my debug-leftovers regex dd\s*\( (laravel dump) matched isQuantityOdd( because the string "dd(" hides inside "Odd(". the tool caught nothing wrong with the fixture and everything wrong with my regex. word boundary fixed it; the test fixture keeps it fixed.

what it is not: an AI detector. it scores diff hygiene signals. a human can write a 100/100 slop diff, an LLM can write a 0/100 clean one. the README lists where the heuristics miss: two-line catch blocks, callers outside the diff, comment patterns in other languages.

github.com/princejain756/slopsieve - npx slopsieve owner/repo#123

what is the one signal you wish your PR queue flagged automatically?

articles.title: Keeping declarativeNetRequest rules in sync after a Manifest V3 service worker restarts
articles.description: By mid-afternoon, my Chrome usually had 40+ tabs open across three windows. I tried several tab...
articles.body_html:
By mid-afternoon, my Chrome usually had 40+ tabs open across three windows. I tried several tab managers, but they either demanded a cloud account, locked basic features behind a subscription, or only solved one half of the problem.

So I spent the last few months building my own: PYLON, an offline-first New Tab that pairs project tab workspaces with dev tools and a deep-focus Pomodoro timer.

This post is about one specific engineering challenge: the site blocker.

The hardest part wasn’t intercepting requests — it was deciding what the source of truth should be when a Manifest V3 background service worker constantly terminates and restarts.

The setup

When a focus session starts, the extension redirects configured distraction sites to a local focus-intercept.html page bundled inside the extension.

I chose Chrome's modern declarativeNetRequest (DNR) API over old blocking webRequests so that the browser itself evaluates rules at native speed without injecting custom JavaScript into the request path.

Three pieces of state have to stay consistent:

What Where it lives Why
Blocked domains chrome.storage.local Survives restarts, handles crashes, easily exported
Active redirect rules DNR Dynamic Rules Evaluated directly by the browser network stack
Rule IDs A reserved ID range (1000–1999) Ensures we only delete focus rules without touching other extension rules

My core rule: chrome.storage.local is the sole source of truth. DNR rules are merely a temporary mirror of it.

Step 1: Clean and normalize user input

Users paste whatever happens to be in their address bar:

  • https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=...
  • reddit.com/r/webdev
  • x.com:443

Because DNR rules match against hostname patterns (typically using ||domain.com^), passing raw URLs will break rule matching. Every entry must be cleaned to a bare domain before touching storage:

const cleaned = Array.from(new Set((domains || [])
  .map(d => String(d || '').trim().toLowerCase()
    .replace(/^https?:\/\//, '')   // drop the protocol
    .replace(/\/.*$/, '')          // drop any trailing path
    .split(':')[0].split('?')[0])  // drop port numbers and query parameters
  .filter(Boolean)));

Step 2: Rebuild the rules — don't patch them

My initial instinct was incremental updates: add a rule when a user adds a domain, remove one when deleted.

In Manifest V3, incremental patching is an anti-pattern.

Service workers can terminate at any point of idle time. If an event wakes the worker while a write is resolving, or if two storage events trigger simultaneously, incremental updates can leave stale, orphaned rule IDs in the browser engine.

Instead, I adopted an idempotent reconciliation pattern:

  1. Read existing dynamic rules.
  2. Filter for rule IDs belonging to my reserved range.
  3. In a single atomic updateDynamicRules() call, delete all stale IDs and re-apply fresh rules generated from storage.
  4. Retry with backoff if Chrome's internal database locks. 
async function reconcileDnrWithStorage(expectedDomains, retryCount = 0) {
  try {
    const existing = await chrome.declarativeNetRequest.getDynamicRules();
    const staleIds = existing
      .map(r => r.id)
      .filter(id => id >= FOCUS_RULE_ID_START && id <= FOCUS_RULE_ID_END);

    await chrome.declarativeNetRequest.updateDynamicRules({
      removeRuleIds: staleIds,
      addRules: buildShieldRules(expectedDomains || [])
    });
  } catch (e) {
    if (retryCount < 3) {
      await new Promise(r => setTimeout(r, 500));
      await reconcileDnrWithStorage(expectedDomains, retryCount + 1);
    }
  }
}

If the focus session ends, passing an empty array automatically clears all rules in that range.

Step 3: Sweeping already-open tabs

One gotcha with declarativeNetRequest: redirect rules only apply to new network requests.

If a user already has YouTube open in a tab and starts a focus sprint, that tab remains accessible until they click a link or refresh.

To make the block instant, the activation sequence performs a quick tab sweep right after reconciling DNR rules:

const tabs = await chrome.tabs.query({});
for (const tab of tabs) {
  if (tab.url && isDomainBlocked(tab.url, expectedDomains)) {
    chrome.tabs.update(tab.id, { 
      url: chrome.runtime.getURL('focus-intercept.html') 
    });
  }
}

Questions for other extension developers:

Building on Manifest V3 has been an interesting exercise in distributed-systems thinking inside a single browser:

  1. Retry Strategy: Is a static 500ms delay sufficient for DNR rule updates, or have you found exponential backoff necessary under heavy browser load?
  2. Reconciliation Frequency: Do you reconcile DNR rules on every service worker startup (chrome.runtime.onStartup), or strictly when storage change listeners fire?
  3. Race Condition Testing: Has anyone established a reliable local testing setup for simulating abrupt service worker termination during active DNR writes?

If you've tackled DNR sync differently, I’d love to hear your approach in the comments.

Try it out:

If you're looking for an offline-first tab manager with native Chrome Tab Groups sync, developer tools (CORS toggle, localhost port monitor), and this focus shield:

👉 PYLON on the Chrome Web Store (Free, 100% offline, zero accounts/tracking)

articles.title: Stripping EXIF and GPS from photos in the browser, losslessly, in ~500 lines of vanilla JS
articles.description: Photos from phones carry more than pixels. Open the file and there's often the exact GPS position it...
articles.body_html:
Photos from phones carry more than pixels. Open the file and there's often the exact GPS position it was taken at, the phone model, lens and settings, the date and time, sometimes the owner's name or a camera serial number, and, increasingly, labels saying whether an image was edited with generative AI.

I make a small Android camera app, and people kept asking whether the photos they share give away where they live. So I built a checker that shows what a photo file carries and saves a clean copy, without uploading anything:

https://blinqdroid.com/tools/photo-privacy-check/

No libraries, no server, no WebAssembly: a DataView over the file's bytes. Here's how it works.

Reading the file without uploading it

The whole thing starts with the bytes in memory:

const u8 = new Uint8Array(await file.arrayBuffer());

From there it's container walking. The first bytes tell you the format: FF D8 is a JPEG, 89 PNG is a PNG, RIFF....WEBP is a WebP, and II/MM at the start is a TIFF (which is also what a DNG raw file is).

JPEG: walking the markers

A JPEG is a list of segments. Each starts with 0xFF, a marker byte, then a two-byte big-endian length:

let p = 2; // skip SOI (FF D8)
while (p + 4 <= u8.length) {
  if (u8[p] !== 0xFF) { p++; continue; }
  const m = u8[p + 1];
  const len = (u8[p + 2] << 8) | u8[p + 3];
  const start = p + 4, n = len - 2;
  if (m === 0xE1 && ascii(u8, start, 6) === 'Exif\0\0') readTiff(u8, start + 6, n - 6);
  // APP1 can also hold XMP: "http://ns.adobe.com/xap/1.0/\0" + XML
  p = start + n;
}

The fiddly part is the image data itself. After a Start of Scan (FF DA) segment comes entropy-coded data with no length field. Inside it, a literal 0xFF byte is "stuffed" as FF 00, and restart markers FF D0–FF D7 can appear. So to find the next real segment (progressive JPEGs have several scans, with tables in between) you scan forward for an 0xFF that is followed by something other than 00 or a restart marker.

EXIF is a tiny TIFF file

The EXIF block is a TIFF structure: a byte-order mark (II little-endian, MM big-endian), the number 42, and an offset to the first IFD (image file directory). Each IFD entry is 12 bytes: tag, type, count, and either the value or an offset to it.

const le = ascii(u8, base, 2) === 'II';
const dv = new DataView(u8.buffer, u8.byteOffset + base);
const count = dv.getUint16(ifdOffset, le);
for (let i = 0; i < count; i++) {
  const e = ifdOffset + 2 + i * 12;
  const tag = dv.getUint16(e, le), type = dv.getUint16(e + 2, le);
  // 0x8769 points to the Exif sub-IFD, 0x8825 to the GPS IFD
}

GPS coordinates are three rationals (degrees, minutes, seconds), each a pair of 32-bit integers, plus a reference letter:

const dms = ([d, m, s], ref) => (d + m / 60 + s / 3600) * (/[SW]/.test(ref) ? -1 : 1);

The IFD after the first one (IFD1) is the embedded thumbnail. It's easy to forget, and it can still show the uncropped original after you've cropped the photo.

PNG, WebP and the AI labels

PNG is a list of chunks (length, type, data, CRC). Metadata lives in eXIf (the same TIFF structure), tEXt/iTXt/zTXt text chunks and tIME. Some image generators write their whole prompt into a tEXt chunk called parameters, so the tool shows text chunks verbatim.

WebP is RIFF: four-character chunk IDs with little-endian sizes, padded to even lengths. EXIF and XMP are separate chunks, and the VP8X header has flag bits saying they're present.

In XMP, the interesting fields for 2026 are the IPTC DigitalSourceType values (trainedAlgorithmicMedia means made with generative AI, compositeWithTrainedAlgorithmicMedia edited with it) and whether a Content Credentials (C2PA) manifest is embedded. The tool only detects C2PA; it doesn't validate the signature.

Cleaning without re-compressing

The easy way to strip metadata is to draw the image on a canvas and export it. That re-encodes the JPEG and loses quality. Instead, for JPEG, PNG and WebP the tool rebuilds the file from the parts it keeps:

  • JPEG: keep everything except APP1–APP15 and COM segments, with two exceptions: the ICC colour profile (APP2 "ICC_PROFILE") and Adobe's APP14, because dropping those changes how colours display. The image data is copied byte for byte.
  • PNG: drop eXIf, tEXt, iTXt, zTXt, tIME and the C2PA caBX chunk.
  • WebP: drop EXIF and XMP chunks, clear their bits in VP8X, and rewrite the RIFF size.

One catch with JPEGs: phones often store the image sideways and add an Orientation tag saying how to display it. Strip all EXIF and the photo shows up rotated. So the clean JPEG gets a brand-new 36-byte EXIF segment containing exactly one tag, Orientation, and nothing else.

Other formats the browser can decode (AVIF, for example) fall back to a canvas re-encode as JPEG at quality 0.95. DNG is read-only, and HEIC can only be cleaned in browsers that can decode it.

Proving it worked

Before offering the download, the page runs the same parser on the clean copy and reports anything left. It's a small step, but it turns "trust me" into "here's what the output contains":

const again = summary(analyse(new Uint8Array(await blob.arrayBuffer())));
const left = ['location', 'identity', 'device', 'time', 'software', 'ai'].filter(k => again[k].length);

Privacy, verifiably

The page runs under a strict Content Security Policy (no inline scripts, no third-party scripts), and the photo never leaves the tab: load the page, switch off your network, and it still works. The script isn't minified, so you can read it at /js/photo-check.js. The only request it makes is to my own page counter, saying that a photo was checked or cleaned. There are no cookies and no photo data in it.

If you find a file it misreads, I'd love to hear about it in the comments: the metadata, not the photo, or a test file with fake details.

articles.title: DuckDB 2.0 alpha's triggers cost three times more per row than per statement
articles.description: I benchmarked DuckDB 2.0 alpha's new triggers on a 500,000-row insert: row-level triggers cost about 3x a plain insert, statement-level ones with transition tables cost about 1.3x. Half the documented trigger matrix isn't implemented yet.
articles.body_html:
DuckDB's preview post for version 2.0 promised triggers with "BEFORE and AFTER triggers, FOR EACH ROW and FOR EACH STATEMENT". I downloaded the alpha build and tried all eight combinations against INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE. Five of them don't work yet, and the one that's missing most completely is BEFORE, which is the half of the feature most people reach for first, to validate or reject a row before it lands.

DuckDB has never had triggers. Version 2.0, codenamed Cyanoptera, is still an alpha, but the CLI binary is a public download, and CREATE TRIGGER already parses and runs for a meaningful subset of cases. I ran the stable 1.5 development build alongside it on the same machine, same data, three repeats per measurement.

$ ./duckdb -version
v2.0.0-alpha46057 (Cyanoptera) b15358c371
$ ./duckdb-1.5 -version
v1.5.7-dev2 (Development Version) 7def715258

What the trigger matrix actually supports

I created the same trigger, varying only BEFORE/AFTER, ROW/STATEMENT, and the event, against a throwaway table:

BEFORE INSERT FOR EACH ROW      -> Not implemented: BEFORE FOR EACH ROW triggers are not yet supported
BEFORE UPDATE FOR EACH ROW      -> Not implemented: BEFORE FOR EACH ROW triggers are not yet supported
BEFORE DELETE FOR EACH ROW      -> Not implemented: BEFORE FOR EACH ROW triggers are not yet supported
AFTER  INSERT FOR EACH ROW      -> works
AFTER  UPDATE FOR EACH ROW      -> Not implemented: UPDATE FOR EACH ROW triggers are not yet supported
AFTER  DELETE FOR EACH ROW      -> works
BEFORE * FOR EACH STATEMENT     -> works, all three events
AFTER  * FOR EACH STATEMENT     -> works, all three events

Every BEFORE row-level trigger fails with the identical error, regardless of event, which reads like the whole BEFORE/ROW combination is simply not wired up yet rather than being event-specific. AFTER row-level triggers fire correctly on INSERT and DELETE, with real NEW and OLD values, but UPDATE gets its own distinct "not yet supported" message. Statement-level triggers work everywhere I tried them, for both BEFORE and AFTER.

I also hit two restrictions that aren't in the preview post at all. You can't mix a FOR EACH STATEMENT trigger and a FOR EACH ROW trigger on the same table:

$ duckdb -c "CREATE TRIGGER trg_stmt AFTER INSERT ON t REFERENCING NEW TABLE AS n FOR EACH STATEMENT ...
CREATE TRIGGER trg_row AFTER INSERT ON t FOR EACH ROW ..."
Not implemented: Mixing FOR EACH STATEMENT and FOR EACH ROW triggers on the same table is not yet supported

And DROP TRIGGER trg_audit;, exactly as written in DuckDB's own blog post, is a syntax error on this build. It needs DROP TRIGGER trg_audit ON t;. Small, but it's the first command a reader would copy-paste and watch fail.

What a trigger costs on a bulk insert

I built three identical tables and inserted 500,000 rows into each with a single INSERT INTO ... SELECT ... FROM range(500000), fastest of three runs:

Setup Time vs. no trigger
No trigger 0.073s —
AFTER INSERT, FOR EACH ROW, logs NEW.id 0.217s (range 0.22-0.36s) 3.0x
AFTER INSERT, FOR EACH STATEMENT, logs the whole batch via a transition table 0.095s 1.3x

The row-level trigger does the same logical work as the statement-level one, one row inserted into a log table per row inserted into the source, but it does it 500,000 times through the trigger machinery instead of once as a set operation. The gap is real and it's the kind of thing an audit-log trigger on a hot table would hit immediately. The statement-level version, which instead references the whole batch at once with REFERENCING NEW TABLE AS n and runs a single INSERT INTO log SELECT id FROM n, is close enough to free that I'd default to it unless I specifically needed per-row logic.

The row-level timings also had the widest spread of anything I measured, 0.22s to 0.36s across three runs against a tight 0.073-0.080s for no trigger at all. Five hundred thousand individual trigger invocations seem to be more sensitive to whatever else the machine is doing than a single set-based statement is, which is its own small argument for preferring statement-level triggers when you can.

I checked that the transition table actually behaves like the docs describe, because the whole cost argument depends on it: does a 10,000-row bulk insert give the statement trigger one transition table with 10,000 rows, or does it somehow get invoked per row anyway?

INSERT INTO t SELECT i, i*2 FROM range(10000) t(i);
INSERT INTO t SELECT i, i*2 FROM range(3) t(i);
SELECT * FROM summary;

| n:BIGINT |
|---|
| 3 |
| 10000 |

One row per statement, with the right count each time. That's what makes the statement-level cost close to flat regardless of batch size.

The one safety check that does work

I tried to get a trigger to fire itself: an AFTER INSERT trigger on t that inserts into t.

CREATE TRIGGER trg AFTER INSERT ON t FOR EACH ROW INSERT INTO t VALUES (NEW.id + 1);
INSERT INTO t VALUES (1);

Not implemented: Recursive trigger chains are not yet supported (trigger cycle detected through trigger "trg" on table "t")

That's a real cycle check, not a stack overflow or a hang. Of everything "not yet supported" in this build, this is the one I'd rather see land unfinished than missing, since the alternative failure mode is a lot worse than an error message.

A claim from the same release that held up better than the trigger matrix

The preview post also claims a rewritten recursive CTE engine, citing a reachability benchmark that went from 4.90s to 0.12s between v1.5.4 and the v2.0 preview. I tried to reproduce something in that shape.

My first attempt was a graph of 100,000 nodes and 1,000,000 random edges, reachability from node 0 via a recursive UNION CTE. It ran in about 0.09s on the 1.5 build. No measurable difference at all, which given the headline claim should have been the first thing I doubted about my own setup, not DuckDB's.

A uniformly random graph with that many edges per node is nearly a complete graph after a handful of hops, so the recursive query converges in a handful of iterations regardless of which engine is running it. It wasn't exercising the part of the engine that changed. I rebuilt the test as a 40,000-node chain, 0 -> 1 -> 2 -> ... -> 39999, which forces the recursion through 40,000 sequential steps and is close to a worst case for any engine that re-evaluates the growing result set on every iteration:

Engine Fastest of 3 runs
v1.5.7-dev2 18.57s (18.57-19.51s)
v2.0.0-alpha46057 0.41s (0.41-0.58s)

About 45x, on a harder topology and at a quarter the node count of their own benchmark. I can't confirm their exact 1M-edge number, but the direction and the rough order of magnitude both check out independently.

What I got wrong on the way

The reachability test above is the mistake, left in rather than quietly fixed. I had a result that said "no difference" and very nearly wrote that down as a finding about the recursive CTE rewrite before checking whether my test actually stressed anything. A graph dense enough to reach everywhere in three hops will look the same on any reasonable query engine; the interesting case is a graph that forces real iteration, and I only got there by being suspicious of a number that was too convenient.

What it costs on disk

v2.0's default storage format moved from version 68 to version 69, and it's a one-way street on this build:

$ duckdb-1.5 v2-database.db -c "select 1"
IO Error: Trying to read a database file with version number 69, but we can only read versions between 64 and 68.

COPY ... TO '...parquet' (FORMAT PARQUET) and reading it back with read_parquet() on the older binary works fine as a workaround, which is how I got the same dataset into both versions for the benchmarks above. Worth knowing before anyone attaches a 2.0 alpha database to data they also need 1.5 to read.

Run it yourself

No Docker needed, both are static CLI binaries:

curl -sL -o v2.tar.gz https://artifacts.duckdb.org/staged/v2.0-cyanoptera/duckdb-cli-linux-amd64.tar.gz
tar xzf v2.tar.gz   # -> ./duckdb

curl -sL -o v15.zip https://artifacts.duckdb.org/v1.5-variegata/duckdb-binaries-linux-amd64.zip
unzip -o v15.zip duckdb_cli-linux-amd64.zip && unzip -o duckdb_cli-linux-amd64.zip   # -> ./duckdb

The trigger cost comparison:

./duckdb /tmp/none.db -c "
CREATE TABLE t(id INTEGER, val INTEGER);
INSERT INTO t SELECT i, i*2 FROM range(500000) t(i);"

./duckdb /tmp/row.db -c "
CREATE TABLE t(id INTEGER, val INTEGER);
CREATE TABLE log(id INTEGER);
CREATE TRIGGER trg AFTER INSERT ON t FOR EACH ROW INSERT INTO log VALUES (NEW.id);
INSERT INTO t SELECT i, i*2 FROM range(500000) t(i);"

./duckdb /tmp/stmt.db -c "
CREATE TABLE t(id INTEGER, val INTEGER);
CREATE TABLE log(id INTEGER);
CREATE TRIGGER trg AFTER INSERT ON t REFERENCING NEW TABLE AS n FOR EACH STATEMENT INSERT INTO log SELECT id FROM n;
INSERT INTO t SELECT i, i*2 FROM range(500000) t(i);"

Time each with time on the command, or wrap it in a shell loop; wrapping the whole duckdb ... -c "..." call is enough since the binary exits when the script finishes.

The chain reachability benchmark:

./duckdb /tmp/chain.db -c "CREATE TABLE edges AS SELECT i AS src, i+1 AS dst FROM range(40000) t(i);"
./duckdb /tmp/chain.db -c "
WITH RECURSIVE reachable(node) AS (
  SELECT 0
  UNION
  SELECT e.dst FROM edges e, reachable r WHERE e.src = r.node
)
SELECT count(*) FROM reachable;"

What to do with this

This is an alpha, so "half the trigger matrix throws Not implemented" isn't a defect report, it's a status update, and most of these gaps will probably close before 2.0 ships. What's worth taking from it now: if you're evaluating triggers for an audit-log or denormalization pattern, default to FOR EACH STATEMENT with transition tables rather than FOR EACH ROW, both because it's roughly 2x cheaper on a bulk load today and because BEFORE row-level triggers, which is where most validation logic naturally goes, aren't available at all yet. And if you're touching the recursive CTE engine for anything that currently needs a manual iterative workaround to stay fast, that part looks like it's already doing what the release notes say, which is reason enough to pull the alpha down and point your own worst-case query at it rather than guessing from a blog post.

articles.body_html:

    • Articles vs. var
    • Gender vs. Typing
  • Languages That Evolve (and Ones That Mostly Don't)
  • Every Language Is a Trade-Off
  • Tell Me About Your Language

How This Started

I've been doing a little research on how good AI models are with uncommon, niche languages. And Georgian, my native language, is my main test subject. Check out the article for more details:

Georgian Language Benchmark: Two Biggest AI Labs Clash in a Language That Doesn't Play by Anyone's Rules
Kaggle Benchmarking Challenge Submission
Giorgi Kobaidze
Giorgi Kobaidze
Oct 11

Georgian Language Benchmark: Two Biggest AI Labs Clash in a Language That Doesn't Play by Anyone's Rules

#devchallenge #kagglechallenge #ai #machinelearning
65 reactions Comments 34 comments
20 min read

While comparing outputs, I kept noticing that the hardest parts weren't vocabulary. They were structure: things Georgian simply doesn't encode that English requires, and the other way around.

And because I'm a developer, my brain immediately filed these under one label: language features. Some features make life easier, some make it harder, and almost all of them are trade-offs.

I'll compare English and Georgian, since those are the only two languages I know (for now, German is in progress). I love both of them, and both are beautiful in their own way. But they couldn't be more different. Georgian has its own alphabet, Mkhedruli, with 33 letters and no uppercase or lowercase in everyday writing. Yes, my native language is case-insensitive by design. We don't really need casing at all.

Let's look at two features.

Feature #1: Articles (or the Lack of Them)

English marks whether a noun is definite (a specific thing the listener already knows about) or indefinite (something new or non-specific). That's the whole job of the versus a/an.

I saw a bus leaving the station. The bus was a white MCI 102-DL3 with silver rims and a Greyhound badge on it.

Georgian has no articles at all. Structurally, the same sentence looks like this:

I saw bus leaving station. Bus was white 1999 MCI 102-DL3 with silver rims and Greyhound badge on it.

In actual Georgian:

დავინახე, როგორ გადიოდა ავტობუსი სადგურიდან. ავტობუსი იყო თეთრი MCI 102-DL3, ვერცხლისფერი დისკებით და Greyhound-ის ემბლემით.

No articles. None. Zero. Null. Undefined.
The listener figures out definiteness from context: what was mentioned before, word order, and the situation itself. The first "bus" is obviously new information, the second one is obviously the same bus.

That doesn't mean Georgian is helpless when it needs precision. It just reaches for other tools on demand:

  • Demonstratives like ეს (this) and ის (that) make something definite:

this/that bus

  • In casual speech, ერთი (one) often works like an indefinite article:

ერთი კაცი შემხვდა ("I met a (certain) man")

The Upside

It's simpler. Fewer words to say and write, and nothing to choose. You never have to stop and think about which article goes where, which is famously one of the hardest parts of English for people whose native languages don't have articles.

The Downside

It's not explicit, and implicit things occasionally become ambiguous. Rarely, but it happens. If someone tells you:

Take bus

Do they mean a bus, any bus, or the bus that's standing right in front of you? In real life, the speaker resolves it with intonation, a gesture, or by saying:

Take this bus

But that doesn't always happen.

And here's where it connects back to my AI research: when a model translates Georgian into English, it has to insert information that wasn't in the source. Every "a" and "the" in the output is a guess. Usually a good one, but still a guess.

Feature #2: Gender

From what I've observed, languages are absolutely obsessed with sorting things by gender. But there are actually two different things going on, and it's worth separating them:

  • Natural gender: pronouns reflect the actual gender of a person. That's English.
  • Grammatical gender: every noun belongs to a class, including spoons, tables, and the moon. That's Italian, German, and many others.

English: He, She, and It

English has he/him/his, she/her/hers, and it/its. That's as far as it goes, and it mostly follows reality: people get he or she, a table is "it". (Except ships, which are sometimes "she" for reasons sailors would have to explain.)

Italian: Two Genders, Every Noun

Italian has masculine and feminine, and every noun has to pick one. There are patterns (nouns ending in -o are usually masculine, -a usually feminine), and then the exceptions show up:

  • la mano (hand) is feminine, despite ending in -o
  • il problema (problem) is masculine, despite ending in -a
  • il sole (sun) is masculine, la luna (moon) is feminine

Logic behind it? Nobody knows. Well, at least I don't. You just memorize them.

German: Three Genders

Think that's complex? German has three: masculine (der), feminine (die), and neuter (das). Look at your dinner table:

  • der Löffel: the spoon is masculine
  • die Gabel: the fork is feminine
  • das Messer: the knife is neuter

Three pieces of cutlery, three genders. It gets better: das Mädchen (the girl) is neuter, because the diminutive suffix -chen always makes a word neuter. Grammar beats biology. And the sun and moon? die Sonne is feminine and der Mond is masculine, the exact opposite of Italian. If gender were logical, the two languages would at least agree on the sky.

I recently started learning German, and honestly, der/die/das is the hardest part for me. The standard advice is to never learn a noun without its article, and now I understand why.

Georgian: Zero Genders

When I was a kid and started learning other languages, this was the weirdest thing of all. Why on earth are words divided by gender? That was absolute nonsense to me. Because in Georgian, there's no gender. None. Zero. Not even for people.

The same pronoun covers he, she, and it: ის (he/she/it), მას (him/her/it, as an object), მისი (his/her/its). The only distinction Georgian makes is between people and things, with ვინ (who) versus რა (what). Which is natural. Nobody asks:

Who is that truck?

The Upside of Gender

It carries information.

My boss is really lovely, she told me I'm doing a great job during the meeting.

One pronoun, and you already know your boss is a woman.

It helps you track references. This is the advantage people rarely mention. In German:

Die Gabel liegt neben dem Löffel. Sie ist schmutzig.

Sie can only be the fork, because the fork is feminine and the spoon isn't. In English, the same sentence is ambiguous:

The fork is next to the spoon. It is dirty.

In Georgian, it's equally ambiguous. Grammatical gender works like a checksum: redundant information that helps the listener connect the right pronoun to the right noun.

The Downside of Gender

What if you don't know?

Tell your boss to give you some vacation days, he or she should be concerned that you're working so much.

Now you have to say both, and it gets clunky fast.

English's escape hatch is singular "they":

When a developer joins the meeting, ask them to show you where the repository is.

One developer, plural pronoun. My first instinct was that this is technically incorrect, but it turns out English speakers have been doing it since the 14th century, and writers like Shakespeare and Jane Austen used it. Even better: English has done this exact trick before. You was originally plural only; the singular was thou. Over time, "you" took over the singular too, and nobody today thinks "you are" is a grammar bug. Singular "they" is the same migration, still in progress.

The memorization tax. For people, gender carries meaning. For spoons and forks, it carries none, yet Italian and German learners still have to memorize it for every single noun.

The Downside of Having No Gender

Georgian's simplicity has a price too. If you want to express gender, you have to say it explicitly: man or woman, gentleman or lady. "My friend" (მეგობარი) tells you nothing about who that friend is.

And once again, this is a real problem for AI. Translating ის into English forces a choice between "he" and "she" that the original sentence never made. Machine translation systems have historically filled that gap with stereotypes: the doctor becomes "he", the nurse becomes "she". Those assumptions are never good.

Complexity Doesn't Disappear, It Moves

Before anyone concludes that Georgian is "easy mode", it isn't. Far from it, it's so complex, sometimes even native speakers struggle to speak or write grammatically correct, It just stores its complexity somewhere else, mostly in verbs.

A single Georgian verb can encode both the subject and the object. მიყვარხარ means "I love you". One word, three ideas. Verbs change form across groups of tenses, and even the case of the subject changes depending on the tense. Georgian dropped articles and gender, then poured all that saved effort into verbs that do an enormous amount of work.

There's a principle in software for exactly this: Tesler's law, or the law of conservation of complexity. Complexity can't be removed, only moved. Languages, it seems, follow it too.

Sounds Familiar, Developers?

All of this reminded me of programming languages, because they face the exact same trade-offs.

Articles vs. var

Georgian's missing articles map almost perfectly onto type inference in C#:

Bus bus = new Bus("MCI 102-DL3");   // explicit: "the bus"
var bus = new Bus("MCI 102-DL3");   // implied, but obvious from context
var next = dispatcher.Next();        // ...is that a Bus? A Route? "take bus"

The compiler always knows what next is. The human reading the code might not. That's why many teams have a style rule along the lines of "use var only when the type is obvious from the right-hand side". It's the Georgian rule exactly: implicit is great when the context makes it obvious, and when it doesn't, you say "this bus" or write the type out.

C# even went in the other direction with target-typed new, where the left side carries the information and the right side drops it:

Bus bus = new("MCI 102-DL3");

Same idea, different side of the sentence.

Gender vs. Typing

German grammatical gender behaves a lot like static typing. Every noun carries a tag, and everything around it (the article, the adjective endings) has to agree with that tag. It's ceremony, and sometimes it feels like noise, but mismatches get caught and references are easier to track.

Georgian pronouns are closer to dynamic typing. ის can hold anything: a person, a truck, an idea. Less ceremony, more flexibility, and meaning gets resolved at "runtime" from context.

C# won't let you mix types without saying so:

int distance = 5;
string label = "2";
var total = distance - label;
// error CS0019: Operator '-' cannot be applied to operands of type 'int' and 'string'

JavaScript will happily guess what you meant:

"5" - 2   // 3
"5" + 2   // "52"
[] + []   // ""

(To be precise, static vs. dynamic and strong vs. weak are two different axes. Python is dynamic but strongly typed: "5" + 2 raises a TypeError. JavaScript is dynamic and weakly typed, which is how you get "52".)

And the arbitrary part of German gender? Imagine a language that forces you to annotate every variable with a type, where the type names were assigned by rolling dice centuries ago, and nobody is allowed to refactor. That's der Löffel, die Gabel, and das Messer.

Languages That Evolve (and Ones That Mostly Don't)

Here's where natural languages and programming languages really differ.

Programming languages learn from each other constantly. C# is a great example. It added generics, then lambdas and LINQ (borrowed from the functional programming world), pattern matching inspired by F# and the ML family, records, and nullable reference types to fight what Tony Hoare called his "billion-dollar mistake". And it doesn't only borrow, it lends: async/await, introduced in C# 5, was later adopted by JavaScript, Python, Rust, and many others.

Natural languages mostly borrow words. English took beef, pork, and mutton from French after the Norman conquest, while the living animals stayed cow, pig, and sheep. Georgian borrowed კომპიუტერი (computer) and ტელეფონი (telephone) like nearly every other language on Earth. Sometimes a borrowed word wins so completely that people forget the original word in their own language ever existed.

The structure, on the other hand, usually stays put. Usually. Natural languages do refactor, just very slowly:

  • Old English had three grammatical genders, just like German. By the Middle English period, they were gone. English deprecated a feature that German still ships today.
  • Thou was deprecated, and you absorbed its job, which is exactly the precedent for singular "they".

The difference is the release process. There's no changelog and no migration guide, a breaking change takes a few centuries to roll out, and every speaker is a maintainer.

Every Language Is a Trade-Off

No matter what design you come up with, there will always be trade-offs. Articles buy precision and cost effort. Gender buys information and reference tracking, and costs memorization. Dropping both buys simplicity and costs explicitness, then the complexity sneaks back in through the verbs.

Every language is beautiful in its own right, and the same goes for programming languages. Learning a new one, spoken or compiled, is the best way to discover assumptions you didn't even know you had. Georgian taught me that a language can live perfectly well without "a/an/the" and "she/he". C# taught me why var needs a style guide. And German is currently teaching me how insanely hard it is.

As for AI: the places where languages disagree on what to encode are exactly the places where models have to guess. Which is precisely why I'm benchmarking them in Georgian.

Tell Me About Your Language

Now it's your turn. What languages do you speak, and how do they handle these features? Do they have articles? Grammatical gender? Is your native language "statically" or "dynamically" typed? Tell me in the comments. I'd love to see which languages follow the same patterns and which break all the rules.

articles.title: AI-Generated Tests Can Agree With the Bug
articles.description: When an AI agent writes both the implementation and its tests, a green build may only prove that the same wrong assumption was encoded twice.
articles.body_html:
An AI coding agent implements a feature, generates tests, runs them, and opens a pull request with a green build.

That looks like independent verification. It often is not.

If the implementation and the tests came from the same prompt, repository context, and interpretation of the requirement, they can repeat the same mistake. The code is wrong. The tests confidently prove that the wrong behavior works exactly as implemented.

The failure is not that AI cannot write tests. The failure is treating correlated output as independent evidence.

The Test Passed Because It Copied the Assumption

Imagine a billing requirement:

Apply a 20% discount to the order subtotal, then add tax to the discounted amount.

The intended calculation is:

subtotal = 100.00
discount = 20.00
taxable amount = 80.00
tax = 8.00
final total = 88.00

An agent misreads the requirement and applies the discount after tax:

export function calculateTotal(subtotal, taxRate, discountRate) {
  const tax = subtotal * taxRate;
  const discount = subtotal * discountRate;

  return subtotal + tax - discount;
}

For the simple values above, both formulas happen to return 88.00. A generated test passes:

import { describe, expect, it } from "vitest";
import { calculateTotal } from "./billing.js";

describe("calculateTotal", () => {
  it("applies a discount and tax", () => {
    expect(calculateTotal(100, 0.1, 0.2)).toBe(88);
  });
});

The test looks reasonable. It even uses a concrete expected value.

But it does not distinguish the intended formula from the incorrect one.

Now introduce a fixed discount, tax exemptions, jurisdiction-specific rounding, or items with different tax classes. The shared assumption becomes a production billing bug.

Coverage Is Not an Oracle

Code coverage answers questions such as:

  • Was this line executed?
  • Was this branch visited?
  • Was this function called?

It does not answer:

  • Was the expected value correct?
  • Did the test encode the product requirement?
  • Would the test fail for a plausible wrong implementation?
  • Did the system preserve a business invariant?

A generated test suite can reach 100% line coverage while asserting the implementation's current behavior back at itself.

This pattern is especially weak:

const result = calculateTotal(order);

expect(result.subtotal).toBe(order.subtotal);
expect(result.tax).toBe(result.taxableAmount * order.taxRate);
expect(result.total).toBe(
  result.subtotal + result.tax - result.discount
);

The test reconstructs the same formula used by the implementation. If the formula is wrong, both sides remain wrong together.

A test needs an oracle: an independent reason to believe the expected result is correct.

Shared Context Creates Correlated Failures

When one agent writes the code and tests in the same session, both artifacts may inherit:

  • the same ambiguous requirement
  • the same incomplete repository context
  • the same mistaken domain assumption
  • the same missing edge case
  • the same naming-driven interpretation
  • the same outdated example

Regenerating the test in the same conversation may not add meaningful independence. The model still sees its earlier reasoning and implementation.

Even using a second model is not automatically enough. If both models receive the same ambiguous prompt and derive expectations from the same implementation, they can converge on the same attractive mistake.

The goal is not merely a different generator. The goal is a different source of truth.

The Dangerous Test Patterns

1. Asserting the implementation against itself 

expect(formatPrice(input)).toBe(formatPrice(input));

This extreme example is obvious, but indirect versions are common. A test may call the same helper, parser, mapper, or formula as the production path.

2. Snapshotting unknown behavior 

expect(calculateInvoice(order)).toMatchSnapshot();

The first snapshot records whatever the implementation produced. Approving it proves that someone accepted the output, not that the output matches the requirement.

Snapshots are useful for detecting change. They are weak at establishing initial correctness when nobody verifies their meaning.

3. Mirroring private implementation details 

expect(cache.internalEntries.size).toBe(1);

The test confirms structure rather than observable behavior. It may pass while users receive stale data, and fail during a safe refactor.

4. Testing only the example from the prompt

If an issue contains one example, an agent will often reproduce it as one happy-path test. That example may not distinguish competing interpretations.

5. Mocking away the failure 

paymentGateway.charge = vi.fn().mockResolvedValue({ status: "paid" });

The test proves behavior for a dependency that always succeeds instantly. It says nothing about timeouts, duplicated responses, uncertain outcomes, or retries after the remote side processed the charge.

A quick review question For every generated assertion, ask: > Where did this expected value come from? If the answer is "from the implementation," "from the agent's earlier output," or "from a snapshot we did not inspect," the test is not independent enough for a critical behavior.

Start With Invariants, Not Examples

Examples verify selected points. Invariants describe properties that must hold across many inputs.

For a discount calculation, useful invariants might include:

  • a discount cannot increase the pre-tax amount
  • a 0% discount changes nothing
  • a 100% discount produces no taxable amount
  • the total cannot be negative
  • changing item order cannot change the total
  • rounding happens at the boundary defined by the business rules

Property-based tests can exercise these rules across generated inputs:

import fc from "fast-check";
import { expect, it } from "vitest";
import { calculateTotal } from "./billing.js";

it("never increases the total when the discount increases", () => {
  fc.assert(
    fc.property(
      fc.double({ min: 0, max: 100_000, noNaN: true }),
      fc.double({ min: 0, max: 0.3, noNaN: true }),
      fc.double({ min: 0, max: 1, noNaN: true }),
      fc.double({ min: 0, max: 1, noNaN: true }),
      (subtotal, taxRate, firstDiscount, secondDiscount) => {
        const lower = Math.min(firstDiscount, secondDiscount);
        const higher = Math.max(firstDiscount, secondDiscount);

        const totalWithLowerDiscount = calculateTotal(
          subtotal,
          taxRate,
          lower
        );

        const totalWithHigherDiscount = calculateTotal(
          subtotal,
          taxRate,
          higher
        );

        expect(totalWithHigherDiscount).toBeLessThanOrEqual(
          totalWithLowerDiscount
        );
      }
    )
  );
});

This still does not prove every domain rule. It does make it harder for one convenient example to hide a broken relationship.

Derive Acceptance Tests From a Separate Source

The strongest acceptance tests should come from artifacts that existed independently of the implementation:

  • product acceptance criteria
  • API contracts
  • regulatory rules
  • protocol specifications
  • previously verified behavior
  • production examples approved by domain experts
  • compatibility fixtures from another implementation

For the billing example, create a decision table before asking an agent to implement it:

Case: percentage discount before tax
Subtotal: 125.00
Discount: 20%
Tax rate: 8%
Expected discount: 25.00
Expected taxable amount: 100.00
Expected tax: 8.00
Expected total: 108.00

Then convert that independently reviewed fixture into a test:

it("taxes the amount after the percentage discount", () => {
  expect(calculateTotal(125, 0.08, 0.2)).toBe(108);
});

The unusual values are deliberate. They distinguish formulas that coincidentally agree for simpler inputs.

Make the Test Fight the Implementation

Mutation testing changes the code in small ways and checks whether the tests fail.

For example, a mutation tool might replace:

const taxableAmount = subtotal - discount;

with:

const taxableAmount = subtotal + discount;

or change:

if (total >= freeShippingThreshold)

into:

if (total > freeShippingThreshold)

If the test suite stays green, it did not protect that behavior.

A mutation score is not a perfect quality metric. Equivalent mutations and costly test runs are real constraints. But targeted mutation testing is valuable for authorization, billing, retries, idempotency, limits, and other logic where a plausible one-character error matters.

Meta reported a related change-aware approach in its 2026 work on Just-in-Time catching tests. Instead of only generating tests that pass on the proposed code, catching tests are designed to surface regressions before a change lands. In an evaluation of 22,126 generated tests, change-aware methods improved candidate catch generation, and the reported process found confirmed serious failures. The important idea is practical: generated tests should actively try to falsify the change, not merely document it.

Use Differential Testing When You Have Two Implementations

Differential testing runs the same inputs through two independent implementations and compares the outputs.

This is useful during rewrites, migrations, and optimizations:

for (const order of generatedOrders) {
  const legacyResult = legacyCalculator(order);
  const newResult = newCalculator(order);

  expect(newResult).toEqual(legacyResult);
}

The reference implementation does not need to be fast or elegant. It needs to be trusted for the behavior under comparison.

Be careful: if the legacy behavior contains known bugs, encode those exceptions explicitly. Otherwise, differential testing can preserve defects just as snapshots do.

Separate the Roles in the Workflow

A safer AI-assisted workflow creates friction between implementation and validation.

Step 1: Extract the contract

Before generating code, write down:

  • inputs and outputs
  • invariants
  • boundary conditions
  • error behavior
  • security constraints
  • examples that distinguish plausible interpretations

Step 2: Generate the implementation

Give the coding agent the contract, but do not let its implementation become the source of expected values.

Step 3: Generate adversarial tests in a fresh context

Provide another agent or session with:

  • the contract
  • the code diff
  • public interfaces
  • known failure classes

Ask it to find counterexamples, not to improve coverage.

A useful prompt is:

Act as an adversarial test engineer.

Given the requirement and code diff:
1. List plausible incorrect interpretations.
2. Create inputs that distinguish them.
3. Identify boundary conditions and invariants.
4. Write tests that would fail for each plausible wrong implementation.
5. Do not derive expected values from the implementation under test.

Step 4: Run targeted mutation testing

Focus on critical decisions rather than mutating the entire repository on every commit.

Step 5: Review the oracle

Reviewers should spend less time asking whether the test is readable and more time asking:

  • Why is this expected value correct?
  • Which wrong implementation would this test reject?
  • Is the test independent of production helpers?
  • What happens at the exact boundary?
  • Which requirement remains untested?

Step 6: Keep merge controls

A green agent-generated pull request still needs repository protections, required checks, and human review. GitHub explicitly requires human review before merging draft pull requests produced by its coding agent and layers security scanning and branch restrictions around generated changes.

That is not ceremony. It is recognition that generated code plus generated tests is evidence, not authority.

A Practical Review Example

Suppose an agent adds this rate limiter:

export function isAllowed(requestCount, limit) {
  return requestCount <= limit;
}

It also generates:

it("allows requests within the limit", () => {
  expect(isAllowed(3, 5)).toBe(true);
});

it("blocks requests above the limit", () => {
  expect(isAllowed(6, 5)).toBe(false);
});

Both tests pass. Coverage may be complete.

But the critical question is whether the fifth request is allowed or whether limit represents the number of requests already consumed. The tests avoid the exact boundary where the interpretation matters.

Add the distinguishing case:

it("defines behavior at the exact limit", () => {
  expect(isAllowed(5, 5)).toBe(false);
});

Whether false is correct depends on the contract. The key is that a human or independent specification must decide it. The implementation cannot decide its own requirement.

Actionable Checklist

Before trusting AI-generated tests, verify that:

  • [ ] Expected values come from a specification, fixture, reference implementation, or reviewed calculation.
  • [ ] Tests do not call production helpers to calculate their own expectations.
  • [ ] Boundary values are tested explicitly.
  • [ ] At least one case distinguishes plausible interpretations of the requirement.
  • [ ] Important behavior is expressed as an invariant where possible.
  • [ ] Snapshots were inspected for meaning before approval.
  • [ ] Mocks include failures, delays, retries, and uncertain outcomes.
  • [ ] Generated tests attempt to falsify the change, not only confirm it.
  • [ ] Critical logic receives targeted mutation testing.
  • [ ] Rewrites are compared against a trusted implementation where appropriate.
  • [ ] A reviewer examines the test oracle, not only coverage.
  • [ ] Agent-created pull requests remain subject to required checks and human review.

CTA: Pick one AI-generated test from your current project and trace every expected value back to its source. If the trail ends at the implementation itself, replace that assertion with an independent fixture, invariant, or boundary case.

The Takeaway

AI-generated tests are useful. They can produce scaffolding, cover routine branches, explore edge cases, and shorten feedback loops.

But tests generated from the same context as the implementation are not automatically independent validation.

They may encode the same misunderstanding twice:

incorrect requirement interpretation
              ↓
      incorrect implementation
              ↓
     matching incorrect tests
              ↓
          green build

Do not measure confidence only by the number of generated tests or the coverage percentage.

Increase independence instead:

  • derive expectations from reviewed contracts
  • test invariants and exact boundaries
  • use fresh adversarial context
  • apply mutation and differential testing
  • review where each oracle came from
  • keep humans responsible for the merge decision

A test suite is valuable when it can disagree with the implementation.

What is the most convincing green test suite you have seen that still allowed a production bug through?

Sources

  • The Death of Traditional Testing: Agentic Development Broke a 50-Year-Old Field, JiTTesting Can Revive It
  • Just-in-Time Catching Test Generation at Meta
  • Risks and mitigations for GitHub Copilot cloud agent
