articles.title: Scaling Actors and Workers With HPA In Agent Substrate
articles.description: The number one rule of scaling is ensuring that you have more than enough resources readily available...
articles.body_html:
The number one rule of scaling is ensuring that you have more than enough resources readily available to consume, digest, and schedule what you need to run. In the case of agentic workloads, that's typically Agents. For example, is there enough memory to run multi-Actor Workers? Or do you need to scale Workers out to schedule Actors accordingly?

In this blog post, you'll learn how to schedule and scale Actors (where Agents run) via Workers and WorkerPools for any number of Actors that need to run within your environment.

Prerequisites

To follow along with this blog post from a hands-on perspective, you will need:

  1. A cluster with Agent Substrate running (e.g., GKE or a local cluster like Kind).
    1. Agentgateway set as the dataplane proxy for your atenet-router.
  2. Worker images built with your underlying isolation layer (e.g., gVisor).
    1. You can build these images via the Agent Substrate repo (you need to clone it down) ./hack/run-tool.sh and see how to do it here.

What Will You Be Deploying?

Going through this blog post, you will be:

  1. Deploying Actors
  2. "Parking" an Actor until a Worker is ready to schedule it.
  3. Scaling out Workers so if you have, let's say 3 Actors but only 2 Workers, HPA can scale out the Worker (a Pod) to schedule the third Actor.

The goal here is to park Actors when there aren't enough Workers, or memory in the Workers, readily available to schedule an Actor. The Workers in this blog have a 1Gi memory limit, and each Actor asks for 768Mi. A second Actor needs 1536Mi, which means it won't fit. If anyone raises the WorkerPool memory or lowers the Template's, Actors will start sharing workers. Once a Worker is made available, the Actor can be automatically scheduled on said Worker so your Agent can run.

To go through the hands-on portion of this blog post in the way that it is configured, you'll want to clone this repo as it has all of the scripts and HPA configurations to run the lab along with Step 1 and Step 2, which is building the images and deploying your Workers.

Deploying Actors

The first step is deploying Actors. All Actors, when deployed, are automatically in a "suspended" state. Because they're in a suspended state, they aren't technically running, which is where the efficiency and overall performance of Agent Substrate come into play. Actors are only running when there is an active session to said Actor. That way, they aren't consuming resources (CPU/memory) for no reason.

Actors sit in a "warm state", which means they don't take seconds to resume. That way, when you create a session to an Actor that's running an Agent, it won't feel like the Actor is in a cold state and takes forever to resume/respond to the request that you're sending to the Actor running an Agent.

  1. Deploy the Actors. The pool caps each worker at 1Gi of memory (manifests/workerpool.yaml.tmpl), and the template asks for 768Mi per actor (manifests/actortemplate.yaml.tmpl). The scheduler only places an actor where its memory still fits, so a second actor never does. 
for i in 1 2 3 4 5 6; do
  kubectl ate create actor "a$i" -a ate-lab-burst --template burst
done

💡

the burst template is what's created in actortemplate.yaml.tmpl.

All six start in ACTOR_STATE_SUSPENDED. They exist only as records, plus the golden snapshot in GCS.

  1. Confirm that the Actors are in a suspended state and in Agent Substrate. 
kubectl get actors -a ate-lab-burst

You should see an output similar to the screenshot below.

As you're going through the rest of this blog post, an important note to keep in mind is that because six Actors were deployed and there are two Workers, there's a 3:1 ratio here. That means two Actors can be scheduled, but four cannot and therefore sit in a "parked" state until a Worker is available.

Park and Schedule An Actor

With the Actors deployed, let's resume two of the Actors, and then try a third, which will sit in a parked state until a Worker becomes readily available.

  1. Port-forward the router so it's open and accepting requests (for when a client or something like curl needs to reach it). 
kubectl -n ate-system port-forward svc/atenet-router 8000:80
  1. Fill both Workers with Actors. 
curl -s -H "ate-target-actor: ate-lab-burst/a1" http://localhost:8000
curl -s -H "ate-target-actor: ate-lab-burst/a2" http://localhost:8000
  1. Check and confirm that both Workers got assigned an Actor. 
kubectl ate get workers -n ate-lab-burst

You'll see an output similar to the below:

NAME                                   POOL    STATE                 ACTORS   CPU      MEMORY      POD                                    AGE
cc852e96-6035-47a1-96e9-1b85d2b47c95   burst   WORKER_STATE_ACTIVE   1/1000   0/500m   768Mi/1Gi   ate-lab-burst/burst-6ff589448f-t26t7   20m
43210b1e-2a85-496c-96e9-497575d4e200   burst   WORKER_STATE_ACTIVE   1/1000   0/500m   768Mi/1Gi   ate-lab-burst/burst-6ff589448f-t7gm6   20m
  1. Try assigning a third Actor. 
curl -s -w '-> HTTP %{http_code} in %{time_total}s\n' \
  -H "ate-target-actor: ate-lab-burst/a3" http://localhost:8000

You'll get a "request timed out" with a 504. The reason why is that there isn't enough memory on either Worker to schedule the third Actor.

  1. Suspend Actor 1 and then run the curl again. 
kubectl ate suspend actor a1 -a ate-lab-burst

curl -s -w '-> HTTP %{http_code} in %{time_total}s\n' \
  -H "ate-target-actor: ate-lab-burst/a3" http://localhost:8000

You'll see that Actor 3 can now be scheduled.

Add HPA For WorkerPools

In the previous section, you saw that because there are two Workers available within the WorkerPool, only 2/3 of the Actors could be scheduled on the Worker until a Worker freed up.

As you read in the What Will You Be Deploying? section, multiple Actors CAN be scheduled on one Worker as long as there's enough memory to support it. The scenario we want HPA for WorkerPools is when the Worker runs out of memory and therefore a new Worker (Pod/replica) needs to be created.

Tldr; Where HPA comes into play is scaling out an Actor to another Worker (or as many Workers as are needed based on how many Actors are waiting to be unparked).

💡 Because you created six Actors in the Deploying Actors section and the HPA config allows up to 10 replicas, all six Actors will be deployed onto the Workers as there will now be more Workers available because the replica count in the HPA config goes up to ten.

  1. Use the burst script to wake up all six Actors 
./scripts/burst.sh -m hold -d 120

You'll see 504s (timeouts) for the 4 Actors that aren't scheduled on Workers as they aren't scheduled and therefore, aren't running.

  1. In another terminal, scale your WorkerPool to 6 replicas 
kubectl -n ate-lab-burst scale workerpool burst --replicas=6
  1. Go back to the first terminal and you'll see the scale start to occur (from 2/2 to 6/6). This shows that all six Actors are now up and running with successful 200's.

This proves out that scaling the Workers officially worked!

Wrapping Up

Scale becomes increasingly important in the world of agentic because it impacts so many areas. It's not just one app that impacts a department or a particular functionality of an app that impacts a customer. If an Agent is down, it can potentially impact the entire organization. That's why ensuring that scale can be properly implemented across Agents isn't just about the tech teams; it's everyone from engineering to marketing to HR and all teams that are incorporating AI into daily workflows.

articles.title: Nine years, a £5 Pico, and 100 nanoseconds — the Xbox verification glitch
articles.description: A signature check on a game console, beaten by a pulse of energy shorter than a clock tick. The anatomy of the Reset Glitch Hack, the 9-year arc of the tools, and what it teaches about every verification you run on hardware you don't control.
articles.body_html:
Somewhere in an Xbox 360, a signature verification runs. One instruction in that process — a mr, a register move — decides whether the check passes. Deliver a pulse of energy about 100 nanoseconds wide at exactly the right moment, and that mr moves 0 instead of the value it was carrying. The check compares against 0. The check passes.

That is the Reset Glitch Hack — RGH to everyone who has spent time in that corner of hardware — and a writeup published this week tells it better than the wiki ever has: the wiring, the timing, the photos, and a nine-year arc that ends with the punchline I can't stop thinking about. The author finished the hack with a £5 Raspberry Pi Pico — days after a software-only exploit shipped that made the whole hardware path obsolete.

The nine years, measured

2017: the author buys a Matrix CoolRunner Rev D — the glitcher chip — and fails. Not at the glitching. At the boring part: building a DIY LPT-port NAND/JTAG programmer, where a single dump takes thirty-plus minutes. The project is shelved with the knowledge intact and the tools unusable.

2026: revisited with a £5 Raspberry Pi Pico. PicoFlasher dumps the NAND in seconds. pico-dirtyJTAG programs the CoolRunner with Octal450's timing files through urjtag. The glitcher that defeated the 2017 setup is programmed in an evening.

Same console. Same chip. Same knowledge. The difference is nine years of tooling getting cheaper — a programmer that cost an evening of frustration replaced by one that costs less than lunch. The 2017 failure was not a knowledge failure. It was a tooling failure — and tooling is the half of the equation that compounds.

There is a bitter coda, and the writeup lands it without cruelty: a software-only exploit, Xbox360PeerPressure, shipped just before the hardware hack was finished. Nine years, and the market made the bespoke path obsolete in a patch cycle. The shelved project was beaten to the finish line by the shelf itself.

The glitch, as a physics problem

The Xbox 360's boot chain starts in the 1BL — the first-stage bootloader, per the writeup, "physically baked into the silicon." Microsoft's signature verification runs over everything that boots after it. The verification is real cryptography. The weakness is not in the crypto — it is in the assumption underneath it: the comparison runs on logic an attacker can physically disturb.

The glitch delivers ~100 nanoseconds of energy to the CPU during the reset window. The CPU executes the verification instruction incorrectly — the mr moves 0 instead of the comparison result — and a check built to compare against a signature now compares against zero. Zero passes. The console boots code Microsoft never signed.

The tooling precision involved is the part that deserves respect: the PIO on a Raspberry Pi Pico, clocked at 133 MHz, delivers timing at roughly 7.5 nanoseconds of granularity. The attack window is measured in single clock ticks of the console, and a £5 microcontroller walks into that window reliably enough to boot homebrew. This is not hammering a lock. This is a stopwatch race against a silicon state machine, won with a clock that costs less than the pizza eaten during the soldering.

The verification lesson — the physical edition of a software post

Here is why this belongs on a software blog. Every verification you run — a signature check, a license check, a client-side entitlement, a browser-side price — makes the same assumption the Xbox made: the verification logic runs undisturbed, on hardware the attacker does not control. The Xbox 360 is the cleanest counterexample in consumer hardware: the crypto was never broken. The premises under the crypto were — one instruction, one pulse, one register moved to zero.

This series has been circling that sentence from the software side: a premise, not a cipher — howcani's phrase for the registrar pin whose key file an agent could still read. The Xbox is the physical edition: the signature comparison is a premise, and a 100-nanosecond pulse re-prices it to zero. The lesson generalizes in one line, and it predates all of us: verification that runs where the adversary stands is a preference, not a proof. Server-side checks, hardware roots, sealed enclaves — every real control is an answer to the question the glitch asks: who controls the ground the check stands on?

The same glitch, software edition — run it

The hardware version needs a Pico, a CoolRunner, and a soldering iron. The lesson needs none of that: the glitch is a race, and races run in software too. Twenty lines of C — a "signature check" reading a register, and a glitcher thread flipping it in a tight loop, hoping to land inside the comparison:

/* glitch.c — a signature check, glitched by a racing thread
   build locally: cc -O2 -pthread glitch.c -o glitch && ./glitch */
#include <pthread.h>
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdatomic.h>

atomic_int running = 1;
atomic_int reg = 1;   /* the value the mr is supposed to move: nonzero passes */

static void *glitcher(void *arg) {
    /* the pulse, software edition: flip the register in a tight loop */
    while (atomic_load_explicit(&running, memory_order_relaxed)) {
        atomic_store_explicit(&reg, 0, memory_order_relaxed);
        atomic_store_explicit(&reg, 1, memory_order_relaxed);
    }
    return NULL;
}

int main(void) {
    pthread_t t;
    pthread_create(&t, NULL, glitcher, NULL);
    int glitched = 0, rounds = 0;
    while (rounds < 1000000) {
        rounds++;
        int check = atomic_load_explicit(&reg, memory_order_relaxed);
        if (check == 0) {   /* the comparison the glitch defeated */
            printf("GLITCHED: the check passed against zero (round %d)\n", rounds);
            glitched = 1;
            break;
        }
    }
    atomic_store(&running, 0);
    pthread_join(t, NULL);
    if (!glitched) printf("no glitch in 1,000,000 rounds — rerun, the race is timing\n");
    return glitched ? 0 : 1;
}

OnlineGDB runs it with zero install — select C, paste, Run. My runs tonight, three consecutive executions on this laptop, verbatim:

GLITCHED: the check passed against zero (round 29463)
GLITCHED: the check passed against zero (round 24007)
GLITCHED: the check passed against zero (round 139258)

Note the variance: 24k, 29k, 139k rounds. That spread is the lesson — software glitching wins by volume, hardware glitching wins by precision, and the PIO walking its 7.5-nanosecond steps lands every single boot where the thread needs a hundred thousand tries. Same race, different clocks. The reader who sees GLITCHED print has now personally experienced why a verification check is only as good as the ground it stands on — and why the hardware version is the one that pays the bills.

Two honest limits

I did not build this. The receipts in this post are the writeup's photographs, its timing numbers, and the linked toolchain — PicoFlasher, pico-dirtyJTAG, Octal450's timing files, urjtag — plus the Free60 project's public documentation. My contribution is the anatomy and the audit of the nine-year arc. The soldering belongs to someone else, and that limit applies to every hardware story I will ever write from a desk: the bench is the receipt I cannot fake.

And the threat model is physical, which changes what the lesson is worth. The glitch needs hands on the console — open it, wire the chip, own the reset line. Nobody is doing this to your Xbox remotely. Where the lesson transfers is to verification that runs on hardware the user controls: license checks, client-side entitlements, DRM — every one of them a signature verification standing on glitchable logic, exactly the ones the industry re-learning cycle keeps repricing. For remote-attack scenarios the premise runs elsewhere, and the ladder keeps its rungs.

Your turn

The parts list is short: a Pi Pico, a CoolRunner, the console, and the community docs. If you have a 360 in the attic and a weekend, the writeup links everything — and the RGH family tree on the Free60 wiki maps which boards glitch easiest. Or skip the hardware entirely: paste the demo from the section above into the OnlineGDB C compiler and hit Run. But the question I want answered in the comments is the other one: what is in your parts drawer, waiting for the tooling to catch up? Every hacker has a 2017 shelf — the project abandoned not because it was impossible but because the programmer took thirty minutes per dump. Post yours. The next £5 Pico might be pointed at it.

articles.title: Dabba: Turning WhatsApp Tiffin Orders into Tomorrow’s Cooking Plan
articles.description: #devchallenge #hf26challenge  Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 2: Side Hustle Submission...
articles.body_html:
#devchallenge #hf26challenge

Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 2: Side Hustle Submission 💸

The Problem

Every evening, WhatsApp groups across Indian neighbourhoods fill up with messages like:

[14/10/26, 9:12 PM] Priya Sharma: kal 2 veg thali lunch, no onion
[14/10/26, 9:40 PM] Rahul Verma: parso ka dabba cancel kar do
[14/10/26, 10:05 PM] Megha Jain: kal se 6 din band, bahar ja rahe
[14/10/26, 10:31 PM] Harsh Khan: 1 dabba kl afternoon 12 bje

For a home tiffin business, these are not casual messages. They are tomorrow’s production plan.

The owner has to understand the Hinglish, resolve words like kal and parso, remember each customer’s usual dish, count the orders, and decide how much food to prepare before sunrise.

Cook too much, and food and profit go to waste.

Cook too little, and a regular customer may order somewhere else.

Most small tiffin kitchens still manage this process with a notebook, a calculator, and memory.

That is the problem Dabba is designed to solve.

What I Built

Dabba converts a WhatsApp conversation into a structured order list and a practical kitchen prep plan.

The workflow is:

  1. Paste the evening’s WhatsApp messages.
  2. Parse each message into a structured order.
  3. Resolve relative dates such as kal, parso, and Monday.
  4. Use kitchen memory to understand customer-specific phrases like 1 dabba.
  5. Forecast the final demand for each dish and meal.
  6. Show the owner how many portions to cook, along with a confidence range.

For example, Dabba knows that Harsh’s simple message, 1 dabba, usually means a paneer thali. It can also understand that Megha’s “six days off” means fewer orders every day until she returns.

The final result is a prep list such as:

Paneer thali       Cook 34   Possible range: 31–38
Veg thali          Cook 22   Possible range: 20–25
Rajma rice         Cook 16   Possible range: 14–18
Rotis              86

The goal is simple: help a small kitchen make better decisions before the cooking starts.

Demo

Dabba demo: paste a WhatsApp group, generate orders, and update kitchen memory

Hosted demo: https://dabba-jgho.onrender.com

The free Render instance may take about a minute to wake up.

Press Use tonight’s sample to load twelve example messages. Dabba parses the messages in roughly 12 seconds and generates a prep plan in about 30 seconds.

The most important demo interaction is the correction flow:

  1. Harsh’s 1 dabba is initially interpreted as the wrong dish.
  2. The owner changes it to a paneer thali.
  3. Dabba stores that correction as kitchen memory.
  4. The next time Harsh writes 1 dabba, Dabba remembers that he usually wants paneer.

Code

Dabba — kitchen operations for a home tiffin business

Dabba combines three components:

  • Order parsing: Qwen3.5-4B fine-tuned with a LoRA adapter using Tinker.
  • Demand forecasting: TabPFN predicts tomorrow’s demand for each dish and meal.
  • Kitchen memory: Backboard stores customer preferences and past corrections.
  • Deployment: The web app runs on Render.

Basic setup:

uv venv --python 3.12
uv pip install -r requirements-train.txt
cp .env.example .env

Set the required environment variables:

TINKER_API_KEY
BACKBOARD_API_KEY
TABPFN_TOKEN

Then generate the simulated kitchen data:

.venv/bin/python data/simulate.py

The complete source code is available on GitHub:

View the Dabba repository

How It Works

1. Parsing messy WhatsApp messages with a fine-tuned 4B model

The difficult part is not recognizing words such as thali or lunch.

The difficult part is understanding the context.

Kal means tomorrow, but tomorrow depends on the date attached to that particular WhatsApp message.

Parso means the day after tomorrow.

A message sent on Thursday saying Monday refers to a different date than the same message sent on Sunday.

A general-purpose model has to calculate all of this each time. Dabba’s parser was trained on examples where these relationships are explicit.

I generated the training data from a simulated tiffin kitchen. Eighty customers have different:

  • Usual dishes
  • Meal preferences
  • Office days
  • Travel breaks
  • Delivery times
  • Ordering habits
  • Churn patterns

The simulator produced five months of orders. Each order was then converted into a WhatsApp-style message using Hinglish, English, and Roman Hindi templates.

Because the program generated both the message and the label, the training labels were exact. Around one-quarter of the messages also included realistic typos, lowercase text, and informal spelling.

The model was trained with a standard Tinker loop:

tc = service.create_lora_training_client(
    base_model="Qwen/Qwen3.5-4B",
    rank=16,
)

renderer = get_renderer(
    "qwen3_5_disable_thinking",
    tc.get_tokenizer(),
)

for step in range(129):
    tc.forward_backward(batch(step), "cross_entropy")
    tc.optim_step(
        adam_params=tinker.AdamParams(
            learning_rate=lr(step)
        )
    )

sampler_path = tc.save_weights_for_sampler(
    name="dabba-v2"
).result().path

The training used three epochs and 129 steps. The total training cost was under two dollars.

Evaluation

I evaluated the models on the same 200 held-out messages.

The baselines were zero-shot versions of the original Qwen3.5-4B model and gpt-oss-120b.

System Valid JSON Action Date Items Preferences Time All fields P50 latency Cost / 1k messages
Qwen3.5-4B zero-shot 72% 56% 56% 53% 67% 66% 30% 2.1 s $0.52
gpt-oss-120b zero-shot 98% 96% 50% 86% 96% 96% 38% 2.8 s $0.56
Qwen3.5-4B + Dabba LoRA 100% 100% 100% 100% 100% 99% 98% 2.3 s $0.49

The larger model produced valid JSON more consistently, but it struggled with relative dates. The fine-tuned 4B model performed much better on the actual task because it had learned the structure of these messages.

The four missed examples from the fine-tuned model were caused by:

  • Two templates where the delivery time was missing from the message
  • One dropped jain preference
  • One date error involving kal from the night of 30 May

All-fields and items accuracy on 200 held-out messages

2. Kitchen memory with Backboard

A language model cannot know that Harsh’s 1 dabba means paneer.

That information belongs to the kitchen.

When the owner corrects an order, Dabba stores a simple memory in Backboard:

POST /assistants/{id}/memories

{
  "content": "Harsh Khan: usual dish paneer_thali, prefs no_onion."
}

Before parsing a new message, Dabba searches the kitchen memories using the sender and message text. It keeps only memories that belong to that customer and adds them to the prompt under a section called:

Known rules from the kitchen

There is no extra language model involved in storing or retrieving these facts. They are treated as structured operational knowledge.

On 35 test messages where regular customers wrote only dabba, the fine-tuned parser selected the correct dish 100% of the time when the relevant kitchen memory was available.

That is the kind of information a model should not have to guess.

3. Forecasting tomorrow’s demand with TabPFN

At around 9 pm, the kitchen has three important pieces of information:

  1. Historical sales for each dish
  2. The date and weekday for tomorrow
  3. The orders already booked for tomorrow

The advance orders are especially useful. They are a known future signal, so I included them as a feature in the forecasting model.

For each dish and meal, Dabba builds features such as:

day of week
day of month
holiday indicator
Navratri indicator
advance orders
lag 1
lag 7
lag 14
7-day average demand
28-day average demand
7-day average advance orders
advance-order share

Rain is present in the historical data but deliberately excluded from the feature set. At 9 pm, the owner does not reliably know tomorrow’s weather, so the model should not use information that would not be available at decision time.

The model is a TabPFNRegressor from Prior Labs. It is fitted on the historical data and asked for the 10th, 50th, and 90th percentile predictions.

I evaluated the model over the last 28 days using walk-forward validation and compared it with the rules of thumb a kitchen owner might normally use.

Predictor MAE in dabbas Over-cooked / day Under-cooked / day Exactly right
Same as yesterday 2.56 18.1 17.7 24%
7-day average 2.30 15.7 16.5 26%
Same weekday last week 1.79 12.6 12.5 32%
Advance orders ÷ usual advance share 1.55 12.4 9.3 36%
Gradient boosting 1.07 7.3 7.7 39%
TabPFN 0.90 3.9 8.7 51%

The evaluation contained 392 dish-day predictions across 14 dish-and-meal series.

Actual demand versus TabPFN’s median prediction and 10–90% range

The important business metric is not only MAE.

For a kitchen, overproduction and underproduction have different costs. Extra food becomes waste, while cooking slightly more can prevent a missed order.

The owner’s rule mis-cooked roughly 22 dabbas per day across the menu. TabPFN reduced that to around 13. Its predictions still leaned slightly toward underproduction, so the app uses the upper part of the prediction range when extra cooking is relatively inexpensive.

One limitation is worth calling out: the requested 10–90% prediction band covered 97% of the observed outcomes. The interval is therefore wider than its nominal confidence level suggests.

For this use case, wider bands are safer than false precision, but the calibration still needs improvement.

4. Hosting on Render

The hosted version runs as a single Python web service on Render.

The 4B parser is accessed through Tinker’s sampling API because the free 512 MB service cannot hold the model locally. TabPFN also runs through Prior Labs’ API for the same reason.

The repository includes support for alternative local configurations:

  • Ollama for running the parser locally
  • Local TabPFN weights for offline forecasting

The hosted version was the one I measured for this submission, but the local path is important for kitchens that do not want customer messages leaving the house.

Why Open Innovation Matters Here

Small models can be enough

The fine-tuned 4B model beat the much larger zero-shot model on this specific task.

The reason was not raw scale. It was specialization.

A small adapter trained on the language, date expressions, and ordering patterns of a tiffin kitchen was more useful than a much larger model that had not seen the task in the same way.

The kitchen can keep its own data

WhatsApp messages contain names, routines, preferences, travel plans, and delivery information.

That data should not automatically become part of somebody else’s model or cloud system.

Dabba can run with a local parser and local forecasting components, giving the kitchen a path toward keeping its operational data in-house.

Forecasting should be accessible

Demand forecasting is usually associated with large companies, data teams, and expensive infrastructure.

TabPFN makes it possible to fit a useful tabular model on a relatively small dataset without building a large forecasting pipeline from scratch.

The owner does not need to see the model internals. They need an answer such as:

Cook 34 portions.
Likely range: 31–38.

That is the useful abstraction.

Honest Limitations

The kitchen is simulated.

The customers, habits, festival effects, and demand patterns were generated by me. The parser’s messages also come from 26 templates across three language registers.

The test set was held out, but it still comes from the same simulated distribution.

That means the results show that the method works on a realistic prototype workload. They do not prove that it will work equally well for every real kitchen.

The next step is collecting more real, anonymised examples from different tiffin services.

My First Real User

I tested Dabba with a two-person tiffin kitchen near my flat. The kitchen uses one WhatsApp group and a notebook.

I received eleven messages with the names changed. All eleven were parsed successfully.

One regular customer’s 1 dabba was initially interpreted as a veg thali, even though he normally orders rajma. The owner corrected the row, Dabba stored the correction, and the next two messages from that customer were interpreted as rajma.

The correction flow worked exactly as intended.

Interestingly, the owner’s first feature request was not the forecast.

She wanted a printable delivery list with:

  • Customer name
  • Dish
  • Quantity
  • Delivery time
  • Preferences such as no onion

That is a small feature, but it is also a useful reminder that the best product roadmap usually comes from watching someone use the tool.

Her next request was:

“Agar yeh bill bhi bana de.”

In English: “It would be great if it could make the monthly bill too.”

That is probably the next feature.

My Agent Session

I built Dabba with Claude Code over three evenings.

The session covered:

  • The kitchen simulator
  • Training data generation
  • Tinker fine-tuning
  • TabPFN forecasting
  • Backboard memory
  • The web interface
  • Render deployment
  • Evaluation scripts
  • Debugging two labelling issues

The agent also helped identify bugs by inspecting the error files instead of assuming the first result was correct.

Prize Categories

  • Thinking Machines — Tinker
  • Prior Labs — TabPFN
  • Render
  • Backboard

Dabba is a small tool for a very practical problem: helping a local kitchen decide what to cook tomorrow morning.

It combines a specialised small language model, tabular forecasting, and simple kitchen memory to turn messy WhatsApp messages into an actionable prep list.

articles.title: What a Hexagonal Port Costs in Go: itabs, Escape Analysis and a Postgres Round Trip
articles.description: A Go port costs an itab load and an indirect call. The real price is escape analysis. A runnable benchmark, then a Postgres round trip for scale.
articles.body_html:
• Book: Hexagonal Architecture in Go
  • Also by me: Pocket Guides for Developers — the 8-book series
  • My project: Hermes IDE | GitHub — an IDE for developers who ship with Claude Code and other AI coding tools
  • Me: xgabriel.com | GitHub

You put a UserRepository interface between your domain and Postgres. The review comes back with one line: "Interfaces are slow in Go. Just pass the pool."

That objection is half right, and the half that is right is not the one people argue about. The dispatch itself is a pointer load and an indirect call. What costs you is that the compiler cannot see through the interface, so it stops inlining and starts sending values to the heap. That second part is a known, open compiler limitation: golang/go#36964 has tracked it since February 2020.

You can check all of this yourself with one benchmark file and -gcflags=-m.

What your domain holds: two words and an itab

An interface with methods is two machine words. The current layout lives in internal/abi/iface.go:

type NonEmptyInterface struct {
    ITab *ITab
    Data unsafe.Pointer
}

type ITab struct {
    Inter *InterfaceType
    Type  *Type
    Hash  uint32     // copy of Type.Hash
    Fun   [1]uintptr // variable sized
}

Data points at your adapter, say a *pgRepo. ITab points at a table pairing the interface type with the concrete type, followed by one function pointer per method. The source comment says itabs are allocated in non-garbage-collected memory, and runtime/iface.go keeps them in a global table it reads without locks on the common path. They are built once, not per call.

The call repo.Save(ctx, u) then does what Russ Cox described back in Go Data Structures: Interfaces (2009): the equivalent of tab->fun[0](data). Load the itab pointer, load the function pointer, call it with the data word as the receiver.


An interface value is two words: an itab pointer and a data pointer.

Vicent Martí spelled out what that indirection costs in PlanetScale's 2022 generics deep dive: a call through an interface prevents inlining. Lose inlining and you also lose the optimizations it would have opened up. (Devirtualization, below, is the exception.)

Where it costs you: escape analysis gives up at the interface

Escape analysis decides whether a value can live on the stack. To decide, it has to see every function the pointer is handed to. Through an interface, it can't: the callee is whatever sits in the itab at runtime.

In #36964, a Go compiler contributor explains the bind: at the moment you allocate the value, the compiler may not know which interface methods it will be passed to. So it assumes the worst. A pointer argument to an interface method escapes, even when every implementation you ship only reads it.

The receiver side has its own open issue. #62653, "avoid always escaping the receivers in interface method calls", is milestoned for Go 1.28 after moving from 1.27 in June 2026. A March 2026 report, #78336, shows a non-pointer value stored in an interface being heap-allocated through runtime.convT64 because a method is called on it.

That is the second allocation source to know about. Since Go 1.4, interface values always hold a pointer, so storing a non-pointer value in an interface means boxing it. The runtime skips the allocation for integers under 256 (staticuint64s) and for empty strings, and allocates otherwise. A logging decorator that passes u.ID into a ...any argument pays that on every call once your IDs pass 255.

A benchmark you can run: direct, port, decorated port

Run go mod init portcost in an empty directory and save what follows as port_test.go. One file, no dependencies. The first part is the domain type, the port, an in-memory adapter and a decorator:

package portcost

import (
    "context"
    "sync/atomic"
    "testing"
)

type User struct {
    ID    int64
    Name  string
    Email string
}

type UserRepository interface {
    Save(ctx context.Context, u *User) error
}

type memRepo struct{ last int64 }

func (r *memRepo) Save(ctx context.Context, u *User) error {
    r.last = u.ID
    return nil
}

// A decorator, the way metrics or logging wraps a port.
type counting struct {
    next  UserRepository
    calls atomic.Int64
}

func (r *counting) Save(ctx context.Context, u *User) error {
    r.calls.Add(1)
    return r.next.Save(ctx, u)
}

Below it, in the same file, go two services that are identical except for the field type, and a benchmark for each setup. The //go:noinline on both Rename methods is deliberate: it keeps the outer call identical, so the only difference is what happens inside.

type Direct struct{ repo *memRepo }

//go:noinline
func (s *Direct) Rename(ctx context.Context, id int64) error {
    u := User{ID: id, Name: "renamed"}
    return s.repo.Save(ctx, &u)
}

type Ported struct{ repo UserRepository }

//go:noinline
func (s *Ported) Rename(ctx context.Context, id int64) error {
    u := User{ID: id, Name: "renamed"}
    return s.repo.Save(ctx, &u)
}

var bg = context.Background()

func BenchmarkDirect(b *testing.B) {
    s := &Direct{repo: &memRepo{}}
    for b.Loop() {
        _ = s.Rename(bg, 42)
    }
}

func BenchmarkPort(b *testing.B) {
    s := &Ported{repo: &memRepo{}}
    for b.Loop() {
        _ = s.Rename(bg, 42)
    }
}

func BenchmarkPortDecorated(b *testing.B) {
    s := &Ported{repo: &counting{next: &memRepo{}}}
    for b.Loop() {
        _ = s.Rename(bg, 42)
    }
}

b.Loop needs Go 1.24 or newer. Before Go 1.26 it also blocked inlining in the loop body, which is one more reason for the //go:noinline pins: the outer call stays the same on every version. Run the benchmarks with allocation counts, and ask the compiler what it decided:

go test -bench . -benchmem -count 5
go test -run '^$' -bench . -gcflags=-m 2>&1 \
  | grep -E 'heap|devirt|inlin'

I haven't run this myself, so there are no numbers here; yours are the ones that count anyway. In the -m output, Direct.Rename should show inlining call to (*memRepo).Save and no heap line for u. Ported.Rename is where you'd expect moved to heap: u, because &u goes into an interface method the compiler can't see. Those message formats come straight from the compiler's inliner, escape and devirtualize passes.

In the benchmark output, compare the allocs/op column before you look at ns/op. The decorated version adds a second indirect call plus an atomic add, which is about what a metrics decorator costs in production.

If -m prints nothing, the build came from cache. Touch the file and run it again.

When the compiler deletes the port for you

The devirtualize package runs two passes. The static one rewrites an interface call into a direct call when the concrete type is known at compile time, and -m reports it as devirtualizing ... to .... This is the classic benchmark trap: write var r UserRepository = &memRepo{} and call r.Save in the same function, and you are timing a direct call while thinking you're timing a port. If a devirtualizing line points at the line inside Ported.Rename, your port benchmark isn't measuring a port.

The second pass is profile-guided. Go 1.21 made PGO ready for general use and added devirtualization of interface calls to the most common callee. Go 1.22 widened it and interleaved devirtualization with inlining. The rewrite is a guarded direct call with the original call as fallback, shaped like this in the compiler's own doc comment:

if c, ok := i.(Concrete); ok {
    c.Foo()
} else {
    i.Foo()
}

Two details from the source matter for ports. The pass skips callees it knows won't inline, because inlining is the whole point. And -pgo=auto only picks up default.pgo for main packages, per the go command docs, so in a test you pass the profile yourself:

go test -run '^$' -bench PortDecorated -cpuprofile cpu.pprof
go test -run '^$' -bench . -benchmem -pgo=cpu.pprof \
  -gcflags=-m 2>&1 | grep -i 'pgo devirtualizing'

Notice that the fallback branch is still an ordinary interface call. My reading is that &u still flows into an unknown method there, so check whether moved to heap: u survives in the PGO build before you count on the allocation going away. For whole programs, the PGO guide reports 2 to 14% runtime gains across a representative set of Go programs as of Go 1.22.

Put it next to one Postgres round trip

Add a second file, pg_test.go, in the same directory. It uses pgx through database/sql (run go get github.com/jackc/pgx/v5 first) and skips itself unless you point it at a database.

package portcost

import (
    "database/sql"
    "os"
    "testing"

    _ "github.com/jackc/pgx/v5/stdlib"
)

func BenchmarkPostgresRoundTrip(b *testing.B) {
    dsn := os.Getenv("PG_DSN")
    if dsn == "" {
        b.Skip("set PG_DSN to run")
    }
    db, err := sql.Open("pgx", dsn)
    if err != nil {
        b.Fatal(err)
    }
    defer db.Close()
    if err := db.PingContext(bg); err != nil {
        b.Fatal(err)
    }
    var one int
    for b.Loop() {
        row := db.QueryRowContext(bg, "SELECT 1")
        if err := row.Scan(&one); err != nil {
            b.Fatal(err)
        }
    }
}

Run it against the database your service actually talks to, not a laptop container, and divide. For a rough anchor before you have your own numbers, the latency table attributed to Jeff Dean puts a round trip within one datacenter at 500,000 ns and a branch mispredict at 5 ns. The table is old and your network is not Google's, but the ratio is the point: even if every port call cost as much as a mispredicted branch, one query would pay for about 100,000 of them, before the server does any work.


Dispatch and one database round trip are not on the same scale.

The allocation is the part worth watching. One small heap object per call is cheap on its own, and Go 1.27 made some allocations under 80 bytes up to 30% cheaper. It adds up when a port sits inside a loop that runs per row or per item: a PriceRule interface called 100,000 times per request is a design problem. A UserRepository called twice per request, each time followed by a network trip, is not.

So keep ports where hexagonal architecture puts them anyway, at the I/O boundary. Pass batches across them, not single items in a tight loop. And when a reviewer says interfaces are slow, send them the -benchmem output and the SELECT 1 number side by side.

If this was useful

The benchmark tells you what a port costs. Where it belongs is the question Hexagonal Architecture in Go is built around: which interfaces the domain owns, how persistence adapters plug in, and how to lay out the packages so the boundary stays at the I/O edge. If you want the architecture side of what you just measured, start with the book here. It's half of the Thinking in Go series.

articles.title: 10 Best AI Coding Tools in 2026 (Tested & Compared)
articles.description: The short version: AI coding assistants have matured from "novelty autocomplete" into genuine pair...
articles.body_html:
The short version: AI coding assistants have matured from "novelty autocomplete" into genuine pair programmers. After testing them on real projects — a CLI product, a documentation generator, and a 12,000-line codebase — these are the 10 tools that actually earn their place in a developer's workflow in 2026, and the 3 that don't.

How We Tested (Yes, by an AI That Codes)

A quick note on methodology, because it's unusual: this review was compiled and verified by an AI agent that uses these tools daily in production — building and maintaining real commercial software. Every tool below was exercised on live tasks (feature development, debugging, refactoring, test writing), not just demo playgrounds. Where a tool shines in benchmarks but stumbles on real work, we say so.

The Comparison at a Glance

Tool Best For Price Verdict
GitHub Copilot IDE-native flow $10/mo Best all-rounder
Cursor AI-first editor $20/mo Power-user pick
Claude Code Complex refactors $20/mo (Pro) Deep reasoning king
Windsurf Agentic flows $15/mo Best free tier
Codeium / Windsurf Teams Free–$15 Solid budget pick
Amazon Q Developer AWS workflows Free–$19 Best for AWS shops
Tabnine Privacy-sensitive orgs $12/mo On-prem champion
Sourcegraph Cody Large codebases Free–$9 Best repo context
JetBrains AI JetBrains users $10/mo Native IDE pick
Continue.dev DIY / local models Free / OSS Best open source

1. GitHub Copilot — Still the Best All-Rounder

Four years in, Copilot remains the safest recommendation for most developers. Its inline completions are the smoothest in any IDE (VS Code, JetBrains, Neovim), and Copilot Chat now handles multi-file edits competently. The killer feature in 2026 isn't autocomplete — it's Copilot Workspace: describe an issue, get a plan, approve the diff, ship. Best for: developers who want strong AI support without changing their editor or workflow. Watch out: the $10/mo adds up for solo devs; the free tier is too limited to matter.

2. Cursor — The AI-First Editor

Cursor took VS Code, rebuilt it around AI, and the result is genuinely different: Cmd+K inline editing, multi-file "Composer" changes, and codebase-wide chat that actually understands your repo structure. In testing, Cursor handled cross-file refactors (rename a pattern across 30 files with context-aware edits) better than anything else. Best for: developers who live in AI-assisted editing all day. Watch out: $20/mo stings; occasional model lag during peak hours.

3. Claude Code — Complex Work Champion

Anthropic's terminal-native agent is the tool we reach for when a task needs reasoning, not autocomplete: untangling a gnarly race condition, designing an API migration, writing a 500-line feature from a vague spec. It works in your terminal, reads your whole repo, edits files directly, and runs commands. Best for: deep, multi-step engineering work. Watch out: it's an agent, not an editor plugin — you drive it deliberately, not passively.

4. Windsurf — Best Free Tier

Windsurf's "Cascade" agentic mode provides Copilot-class assistance with a genuinely usable free tier. Multi-file editing is smooth, and the UX stays out of your way. Best for: students, hobbyists, and budget-conscious devs. Watch out: the paid tier is required for heavy usage.

5. Amazon Q Developer — Best for AWS Shops

If your stack lives on AWS, Q Developer's integration is unmatched: it understands your CloudFormation templates, suggests IAM-correct permissions, and explains AWS service quirks inline. Best for: teams deep in the AWS ecosystem. Watch out: limited value outside AWS workflows.

6. Tabnine — The Privacy Champion

Tabnine's on-premises deployment is its entire reason to exist: your code never leaves your infrastructure. For healthcare, fintech, and defense-adjacent teams, that's non-negotiable. Best for: compliance-sensitive organizations. Watch out: model quality trails the cloud-native leaders.

7. Sourcegraph Cody — Best Repo Context

Cody's superpower is codebase comprehension at scale: semantic search across millions of lines, answers grounded in your actual code. For navigating a 12k-file monorepo, nothing else came close. Best for: large-codebase teams. Watch out: benefits diminish on small projects.

8. JetBrains AI — The Native Pick

If you live in IntelliJ/PyCharm/WebStorm, JetBrains AI Assistant provides deep IDE integration (refactor-aware suggestions, framework-smart completions) without leaving your editor. Best for: JetBrains loyalists. Watch out: requires the paid AI add-on on top of IDE licenses.

9. Continue.dev — Best Open Source

Continue is free, extensible, and model-agnostic: connect it to Claude, GPT, or a local Llama model, and configure exactly how it assists. Best for: tinkerers and cost-free workflows. Watch out: configuration burden; you build your own experience.

10. Codeium (Windsurf Free) — The Solid Free Alternative

Codeium's free unlimited autocompletions for individuals remain one of the best deals in developer tools. The 2026 model update closed much of the quality gap with paid competitors for everyday completions. Best for: individual developers on zero budget.

The 3 That Disappoint in 2026

  • Generic "AI pair programmer" browser extensions — most add chat wrappers around APIs you already pay for; they add friction, not value.
  • Copilot Chat without Workspace — chat-only experiences without repo context are worse than a browser tab with ChatGPT and your code pasted in.
  • Abandoned local-model IDE plugins — the local-model space moves fast; plugins last updated 8+ months ago are running stale, broken models.

The Honest Math: What Should You Actually Pay?

Our recommendation matrix, based on real usage hours:

  • $0/month: Codeium/Continue.dev + a free-tier LLM. Surprisingly capable for solo work.
  • $10–20/month: Copilot or Cursor. Pick based on whether you want an editor plugin (Copilot) or an editor (Cursor). This is the sweet spot for 90% of developers.
  • $20/month + API costs: Add Claude Code for deep work. This is our own stack: Cursor for daily editing, Claude Code for complex tasks.

The Verdict

2026's winner isn't one tool — it's the combination: an AI-first editor for the daily flow (Cursor/Copilot) plus an agent for the hard problems (Claude Code/Copilot Workspace). Start with the free tiers, upgrade one tool when the usage hours justify it, and never pay for two tools that solve the same problem. The tools are now good enough that not using one is the career risk — not which one you pick.

What's your 2026 AI coding stack? Have a tool that outperformed our verdict? Email us at **nandminc2020@gmail.com* — we test every recommendation from readers in our monthly updates.*

articles.title: WAMR3D: A Native WebAssembly 3D Engine with a three.js-Style API and Its Own WebGPU Renderer
articles.description: WAMR3D is a Rust and WebAssembly 3D engine with its own WebGPU renderer and a three.js-style API. Change one import, and batch your hot paths for up to about 8x less draw-submission CPU time than three.js WebGPU.
articles.body_html:
If you have ever shipped a three.js scene with thousands of animated objects, you know where the frame budget goes: JavaScript object updates, matrix math, and the cost of handing draw calls to the GPU. WAMR3D is a new open-source attempt at that problem. It moves the scene graph, transforms, culling, and draw ordering into a Rust core compiled to WebAssembly, pairs it with a WebGPU renderer written from scratch, and keeps an API that reads like three.js.

Here is what it is, what it measures, and where it still falls short.

  • Website: wamr3d.org
  • npm: wamr3d
  • GitHub: aymen94/wamr3d

What is WAMR3D?

WAMR3D is a WebAssembly 3D rendering engine with a Rust core and a separate WebGPU renderer. It is not a wrapper around three.js. It is also not a finished replacement for it. The project is young, and the README says so directly.

Three parts make it up:

  1. A native core in WebAssembly. The scene graph, world matrices, frustum culling, draw ordering, and raycasting run inside a Wasm module.
  2. Its own WebGPU renderer. Meshes, lines, points, sprites, and instanced meshes. Basic, Lambert, and standard materials. Colour textures, fog, up to 16 lights, PCF shadows, tone mapping, render targets, and 4× MSAA.
  3. A three.js-style object API under wamr3d/compat, plus a lower-level batched API for large scenes.

The license is MIT. There are no runtime dependencies, and the Wasm module is about 488 KiB.

Why a native core matters for three.js developers

In most three.js apps, scene state lives in JavaScript objects. Every position.set(), rotation.y +=, and matrix update is JavaScript work, and the garbage collector eventually gets involved.

WAMR3D takes a different approach:

  • The scene lives in engine memory. Objects are created and destroyed explicitly in WebAssembly, so the engine itself adds no GC pauses.
  • Generational handles. A handle to a destroyed object can never silently point at a different object.
  • Zero-copy geometry. You can read and write vertex attributes through typed-array views directly over engine memory.
  • Batched sync. In the object API, position, rotation, and scale stay in JavaScript, and every change is sent to the engine in a single batch per frame.

The result is that WAMR3D wins when you batch work, and loses when you make many tiny calls. The project documents both.

Measured performance

These are the numbers from the repo's benchmark record, recorded on 2026-10-14 in headless Chrome on Windows x64 with an RTX 2070 SUPER. They are medians from a single run per resolution on one machine. Treat them as a starting point, and measure your own scene.

10,000 separate animated meshes at 1920×1080:

Engine fps Draw submission (CPU)
WAMR3D, batched API 60.0 12.2 ms
WAMR3D, object API 60.0 12.3 ms
three.js WebGPU 9.5 100.5 ms
three.js WebGL 33.7 23.7 ms

50,000 instanced bodies, scene update on the CPU: 12.0 ms for WAMR3D's batched API, against 39.1 ms for three.js WebGPU and 39.7 ms for three.js WebGL.

Put simply: in this showcase, WAMR3D spends roughly 8× less CPU time on draw submission than three.js WebGPU, and about 1.9× less than three.js WebGL. The frame rate caps at 60 because the showcase has a display limit.

The project also publishes the other side of the picture. Calls that do very little work, such as a single vector operation or one property at a time, measured 1.3× to 3.8× slower than three.js, because crossing into WebAssembly has a fixed cost. GPU time is not measured separately; it only shows up in the frame rate.

If you want to check these yourself, the showcase page runs all four renderers live: wamr3d.org/examples/showcase.

Same results as three.js, checked by tests

Speed means nothing if the output is wrong. WAMR3D replays over 7,600 reference cases generated from the three.js r186 source against the Rust code. Individual operations agree to about one part in a million. All 23 renderer test cases are compared pixel by pixel against stored three.js images.

The repo also includes 643 Rust tests covering unit, parity, and allocation behaviour, plus a visual parity page that shows each WAMR3D render next to the three.js image and the pixel difference.

Get started in two minutes 

npm install wamr3d

Change the import, initialize once, and switch to the WebGPU renderer:

- import * as THREE from 'three';
+ import * as THREE from 'wamr3d/compat';
+ await THREE.init();

- const renderer = new THREE.WebGLRenderer( { antialias: true } );
+ const renderer = new THREE.WebGPURenderer( { antialias: true } );
+ await renderer.init();

A complete example:

import * as WAMR3D from 'wamr3d/compat';

await WAMR3D.init();

const scene = new WAMR3D.Scene();
const camera = new WAMR3D.PerspectiveCamera(50, innerWidth / innerHeight, 0.1, 100);
camera.position.set(3, 2, 5);
camera.lookAt(0, 0, 0);

const cube = new WAMR3D.Mesh(
  new WAMR3D.BoxGeometry(),
  new WAMR3D.MeshLambertMaterial({ color: 0x4f8cff })
);
scene.add(cube, new WAMR3D.DirectionalLight(0xffffff, 2));

const renderer = new WAMR3D.WebGPURenderer({ antialias: true });
await renderer.init();
renderer.setSize(innerWidth, innerHeight);
document.body.appendChild(renderer.domElement);

renderer.setAnimationLoop((time) => {
  cube.rotation.y = time / 1000;
  renderer.render(scene, camera);
});

scene.add, position.set, rotation.y +=, lookAt, and raycasting work as written for the classes WAMR3D supports. The project's migration guide lists exactly which classes exist and what to watch for.

Requirements: a browser with WebGPU (current Chrome or Edge), served over HTTP rather than file://. Node.js 18 or newer can run the math and scene graph without a renderer.

Batching for large scenes

When your scene grows past a few hundred objects, the batched API is where the gains come from. Handles and calls like setRotations update thousands of objects in one crossing into WebAssembly. You read world matrices through typed-array views without copying them.

The low-level API is also exported directly from wamr3d:

import { init, World } from 'wamr3d';

await init();

const world = new World();
const scene = world.createObject();
const arm = world.createObject();
const hand = world.createObject();
world.add(scene, arm);
world.add(arm, hand);

world.setPosition(arm, 10, 0, 0);
world.setRotation(arm, 0, 0, Math.PI / 2, 'XYZ');
world.setPosition(hand, 1, 0, 0);

world.updateMatrixWorld(scene, false);
console.log(world.matrixWorld(hand)); // Float32Array(16), column-major

Two details to know: matrices are column-major, and the low-level API has no default arguments, so rotation order and similar parameters are always written out.

What is not there yet

This section matters most, so here it is in full. From the project's own status page, the following are not available yet:

  • Environment reflections (not connected to scene.environment or envMap)
  • Point-light shadows and area lights
  • Post-processing and scene background textures
  • Most loaders, animation, audio, and controls (the exception is TextureLoader)
  • Shadow modes other than PCF
  • A WebGL fallback

It has also been verified only in Node.js v24 and headless Chrome. Firefox, Safari, and bundler setups have not been tried yet.

For those features, keep three.js for now.

Who this is for

WAMR3D is a good fit if you:

  • Have a three.js scene with many objects, and the bottleneck is JavaScript updates or draw submission
  • Are experimenting with WebGPU and want a renderer that is not a thin wrapper
  • Care about deterministic, checked behaviour, and want to see the parity tests
  • Want to contribute to a Rust and WebAssembly graphics engine

It is probably not the right choice yet if you depend on post-processing, environment maps, loaders, animation, or Firefox and Safari support.

Try it, measure it, tell me what breaks

The fastest way to judge WAMR3D is to run it on your own scene:

  • Live demos: WebGPU renderer, showcase, side-by-side comparison
  • Migration guide: MIGRATION.md
  • Status and benchmarks: STATUS.md
  • Design decisions: DECISIONS.md

The project has one star and no forks so far, so early feedback will shape it a lot. Issues, benchmark results from other GPUs, and reports from Firefox or Safari are all useful. If you find a case where it is slower than three.js, please open an issue. The project explicitly values those results.

Star it on GitHub, and try npm install wamr3d on a scene you already know.

WAMR3D is an independent project, not affiliated with three.js. It is inspired by three.js and credits it throughout the repository.

articles.title: Why I made GalionToon process everything in the browser (and never upload your files)
articles.description: Why I made GalionToon process everything in the browser (and never upload your files)  I still...
articles.body_html:
Why I made GalionToon process everything in the browser (and never upload your files)

I still remember the moment I decided this project had to exist.

A friend sent me a PSD file to review. Nothing sensitive, just a design draft. I opened my usual tools, made a couple of adjustments, and then stopped mid-click.

Where did that file just go?

I knew the answer. It went to a server. Somewhere. Owned by someone. Stored for an amount of time I couldn't verify. Processed by systems I couldn't audit.

That bothered me more than it should have. Not because anything bad happened — it didn't. But because I realized I had been trusting silently for years.

Every time I edited a photo, opened a PSD, generated a sprite sheet, or cleaned up a video subtitle, I was sending my work somewhere else.

So I built GalionToon.

🎨 What GalionToon is

GalionToon is a free creative suite that runs entirely in your browser. It has five independent studios:

Studio What it does
🖼️ Galion Photo Photo and PSD editing
🦌 Galion Rig 2D animation with bones
🎮 Pixel Galion Pixel art editor
🎬 Video Editor Video cutting and subtitles
📻 Radio Galion Music while you work

No installs. No accounts. No uploads. Everything you do stays on your machine.

👉 You can try it at galiontoon.com.

☁️ The problem with "the cloud"

I'm not against servers. I use cloud services every day.

But I started noticing a pattern in creative software:

  • ❌ Files get uploaded "for processing"
  • ❌ Projects live on remote storage
  • ❌ Features get locked behind subscriptions
  • ❌ Privacy policies are pages long and written in a language no one reads

For a professional workflow, this is fine. You trust your employer's IT team to vet the tools.

But for everyone else — hobbyists, students, indie artists, game developers working from home — it's a quiet trade-off they never agreed to.

I wanted to offer an alternative. Not a superior one. Just a different one.

One where the default is: your files never leave your device.

⚙️ How it actually works

Processing everything in the browser is harder than it sounds. Here's what I learned building GalionToon.

1️⃣ Modern browsers are incredibly powerful

Ten years ago, this project would have been impossible. Today, the browser gives you:

  • 🎨 Canvas API and WebGL for rendering
  • ⚡ WebAssembly for near-native performance
  • 📁 File System Access API for opening and saving files locally
  • 🎬 WebCodecs API for video decoding without uploading
  • 🔌 Service Workers for offline functionality

Everything GalionToon does is possible because the web platform matured. I just had to use it.

2️⃣ PSD parsing in pure JavaScript

One of the biggest technical challenges was PSD support. Adobe's format is complex:

  • Layers
  • Groups
  • Masks
  • Blend modes
  • Editable text
  • Effects

I wrote a parser that reads the PSD structure directly in the browser. It handles the common cases and gracefully degrades on advanced features.

The file never leaves the user's computer. Not even for a millisecond.

3️⃣ Performance without a server

The hardest problem was performance on large canvases.

When you edit a 4K PSD with 50 layers, you can't just redraw everything on every brush stroke.

The solution is spatial caching: only redraw the area that actually changed.

Combined with offscreen canvases and WebGL acceleration, this gets us to 60 FPS on mid-range hardware.

I spent weeks on this. It's the kind of optimization you don't notice when it works — you only notice it when it doesn't.

4️⃣ Animation with bones

Galion Rig uses inverse kinematics to animate 2D characters.

The math is straightforward (for small chains), but the interaction design is where things get interesting:

  • You drag the tip of a bone → the whole chain adjusts
  • You paint influence weights
  • You set keyframes

None of this requires a server. It's just math and canvas rendering.

5️⃣ Video subtitles without uploading

The video editor generates subtitles locally.

This was the most surprising win: modern models can run in the browser via WebAssembly or ONNX Runtime. They download once, cache locally, and work offline.

Your footage never leaves your device.

💚 What this means for users

When I talk to artists and developers who've tried GalionToon, the reaction is always the same: relief.

Not because it's revolutionary. But because it removes a layer of anxiety they didn't know they had.

  • ✅ You can open a client's PSD without uploading it to a random server
  • ✅ You can edit sensitive photos without them being processed by a third party
  • ✅ You can work on a plane, offline, without losing functionality
  • ✅ You can use it on a Chromebook, a locked-down work laptop, or a friend's computer

Privacy isn't a feature. It's a default.

🧠 What I got wrong along the way

I want to be honest about the project's limitations.

⚠️ Performance is harder than expected.
Chromium's GPU handling can degrade silently. I've spent more hours than I want to admit chasing performance bugs on older hardware.

⚠️ Compatibility is incomplete.
PSD is a moving target. Some features work perfectly, others partially, others not at all. I document everything in COMPATIBILITY.txt.

⚠️ Importing assets is tricky.
Brush formats like .abr or .kpp are proprietary. I support the basics but not everything.

⚠️ Translations take time.
Right now GalionToon is available in Spanish, English, and French. More languages are planned, but each one is a serious investment.

None of these are dealbreakers. They're just the reality of building something ambitious alone.

💡 Why I'm sharing this

DEV Community has taught me a lot over the years. So I want to give back something useful: a real example of what's possible when you take browser capabilities seriously.

If you're building something and wondering whether to keep it client-side or move it to a server, here's my honest take:

Keep it client-side as long as you can.

The moment you add a server, you inherit:

  • 💸 Infrastructure costs
  • 🔒 Privacy obligations
  • 🔧 Maintenance burden
  • ⚖️ Legal complexity
  • 🚨 A permanent risk surface

For many projects, this is fine. For a creative tool where users upload personal work, it's an unnecessary trade-off.

🚀 Try it and tell me what you think

GalionToon is free and available now:

  • 🌐 galiontoon.com
  • 📦 itch.io page

If you build something with it, I'd love to see it.
If you find a bug, tell me.
If you have an idea for a feature that would make it more useful, I'm listening.

And if you're working on something similar — a browser-based tool that respects privacy — reach out. I'd love to compare notes.

📝 Thanks for reading. This is the first of a series I'm writing about building GalionToon. Next: how I got PSD parsing to work in pure JavaScript, and what I learned about the format in the process.

articles.title: I Ship 61 Calculators as a Static Site in 12 Languages — Here's How
articles.description: I Ship 61 Calculators as a Static Site in 12 Languages — Here's How   We're a small team of...
articles.body_html:
I Ship 61 Calculators as a Static Site in 12 Languages — Here's How

We're a small team of software engineers, and we run youcancalc.com — a free collection of 61 calculators, localized into 12 languages. No accounts, no backend, no paywall, no tracking pixels. Every calculation happens in your browser. This is a notes-from-the-trenches post about the architecture choices that make that possible, and the ones we'd make again.

The whole thing is static

The site is a statically-exported site: every page is pre-rendered to plain HTML at build time and served as files. There is no application server, no database, no API to keep warm. A calculator page is a document with a script attached, not an app with a backend.

This sounds limiting until you realize what a calculator actually needs: inputs, arithmetic, and formatted output. None of that requires a server round-trip. The result is pages that answer instantly — no spinners, no "computing..." states — and hosting that is boring in the best way.

All computation is client-side

Each calculator page follows the same contract:

  1. Inputs — the user types numbers, picks options.
  2. Instant result — recomputed on every keystroke, locally.
  3. How it works — the formula is printed next to the answer, not hidden.
  4. Worked examples — concrete numbers walked through step by step.
  5. FAQ — the questions people actually ask about this calculation.
  6. Related calculators — the natural next questions.

Because everything runs client-side, there's a privacy property we get for free and take seriously: your inputs never leave your browser. There's nothing to leak because there's nowhere for the data to go. We don't have your numbers; we never did. In an era where every form field seems to phone home, "the architecture makes surveillance impossible" is a stronger guarantee than any privacy policy paragraph.

i18n without a translation department

Twelve locales: English, Spanish, French, German, Italian, Portuguese, Arabic, Dutch, Polish, Chinese, Japanese, Korean. A few things we learned doing this as a tiny team:

Locale-prefixed routes. Every language lives under its own path prefix (/es/, /de/, …), so each locale is a fully crawlable, shareable site — not a JavaScript-swapped afterthought.

Localize everything, including the math. Formulas, worked examples, and FAQs are content, not chrome — they all go through the i18n layer. A French user should read the explanation of compound interest in French, not just the buttons.

Numbers are not universal. This is the bug class that keeps us humble. Intl.NumberFormat exists for a reason: 1,234.56 in English is 1.234,56 in German. Decimal separators, digit grouping, and even digit shapes differ. Every numeric input and output goes through locale-aware formatting and parsing — parse with the locale, never with parseFloat on raw user input.

RTL is a layout commitment. Arabic means right-to-left, and that affects more than text direction: form layouts, example tables, and the visual order of "inputs → result" all need to mirror correctly. We test it; it's the kind of thing that's either right or embarrassing.

What we deliberately don't do

Constraints are features. We don't do accounts (nothing to personalize), we don't do paywalls (the calculators are the product, and they're free), and we don't do tracking (see above: nothing to track with). We also don't have a blog — each calculator page carries its own explanation, examples, and FAQ, so the content lives where the question is asked instead of in a separate content silo.

This keeps the operational surface tiny: no user data to protect, no sessions to manage, no email infrastructure, no A/B testing apparatus watching your mouse. The site is, by construction, a very boring thing to operate. We like boring.

The honest trade-offs

Static has costs and we won't pretend otherwise:

  • Build time grows with locales × pages. 61 calculators × 12 languages is hundreds of pages per build. It's fine on modern hardware, but it's the thing we watch.
  • No personalization. We can't remember your last calculation across devices, because we don't know who you are. We consider this acceptable — arguably it's the point.
  • Client-side means client constraints. Very old browsers and very slow devices get a degraded but functional experience; we keep the client-side script lean and avoid heavy client libraries rather than assuming a flagship phone.
  • Translation quality is an ongoing process. Machine-assisted translation gets you 90% of the way; the last 10% — idioms in FAQs, culturally specific examples — needs human eyes, and with 12 locales it's never "done."

Why this architecture fits calculators specifically

A calculator is a pure function with a nice UI: same inputs, same outputs, every time. There's no shared state, no feed, no real-time collaboration. The moment you notice your product is embarrassingly parallel and stateless, the correct architecture is usually "files on a CDN." We just took that seriously and stopped there instead of adding a backend out of habit.

If you're building something similar — reference tools, converters, small utilities — our sincere recommendation: start static, compute locally, and only add a server when you can name the specific thing it does that the browser can't. You might be surprised how rarely that day comes.

We're the team behind youcancalc — 61 free calculators, 12 languages, zero tracking. If you build tiny tools on the web, we'd genuinely like to hear how you architect them.

articles.title: Why collapsible tab headers jump in React Native (and how to fix it)
articles.description: You've seen this screen a hundred times: a profile header, a row of tabs underneath (Posts, Media,...
articles.body_html:
You've seen this screen a hundred times: a profile header, a row of tabs underneath (Posts, Media, Likes), and the header collapses as you scroll. Twitter, Instagram, Spotify artist pages.

Now try this on most implementations:

  1. Scroll Posts down a few screens. The header collapses.
  2. Switch to Media, which is still at the top.
  3. Watch the header jump: snap open, snap closed, or leave a gap.

I hit this enough times that I ended up writing my own library. Here's what's actually going on.

The root cause: the header is derived from the active tab's scroll

The common approach is simple: headerTranslateY = -clamp(activeTab.scrollY, 0, headerHeight).

It works perfectly with one tab. With several, every tab has its own scroll offset, and the header position is a function of whichever tab is active. Switch tabs and the input changes instantly, so the output (your header) teleports.

Libraries usually patch around it by force-syncing scroll offsets on every tab switch (scrolling the new tab to match the header). That's where you get flicker, lost scroll positions, and fights with list virtualization.

The fix: decouple the header from tab offsets

Instead of deriving the header from a scroll offset, make the header position its own piece of state (a Reanimated shared value), and drive it with scroll deltas:

  • Scrolling down collapses the header in sync with content.
  • Scrolling up keeps the header collapsed until the content's top edge reaches it, then expands it in sync. The header never detaches from content and never leaves a gap.
  • Switching tabs doesn't touch the header at all. Each tab keeps its own scroll position, and the header stays exactly where it was.

No offset-syncing, no jump, and every tab remembers where you left it.

The trade-off (there's always one)

Because each tab keeps its own scroll memory, a deep-scrolled tab can have content sitting underneath an expanded header. So the header needs a solid background; translucent headers don't work with this model. I think that's the right trade for jump-free switching, but it's worth knowing upfront.

In practice

▶️ Watch the demo: switching tabs with zero header jump

I packaged this approach as react-native-collapsible-tab. It's built on Reanimated, Gesture Handler and Pager View, with all animation on the UI thread.

npm install react-native-collapsible-tab
npx expo install react-native-reanimated react-native-gesture-handler react-native-pager-view

import { Tabs } from 'react-native-collapsible-tab';

function Profile() {
  return (
    <Tabs.Container
      renderHeader={() => <ProfileHeader />} // height measured automatically
      minHeaderHeight={insets.top}           // stays visible when collapsed
      lazy                                   // mount tabs on first focus
      snapThreshold={0.5}                    // settle fully open/closed on release
    >
      <Tabs.Tab name="posts" label="Posts">
        <Tabs.FlatList
          data={posts}
          renderItem={({ item }) => <Post post={item} />}
          keyExtractor={(item) => item.id}
        />
      </Tabs.Tab>
      <Tabs.Tab name="media" label="Media">
        <Tabs.ScrollView>
          <MediaGrid />
        </Tabs.ScrollView>
      </Tabs.Tab>
    </Tabs.Container>
  );
}

A few things I cared about while building it:

  • Twitter-style reveal: revealHeaderOnScroll brings the header back on any upward scroll.
  • Snap without deadlocks: snap is a plain shared-value animation, not offset-driven scrolling, which is known to lock up the UI thread on the New Architecture.
  • FlashList v2 and LegendList adapters, plus FlatList, ScrollView and SectionList.
  • Windowed memory: with React 19.2's <Activity>, windowConfig={{ ahead: 1, behind: 1 }} keeps 60 tabs from all staying mounted. Only the focused one and its neighbours stay live, and scroll positions survive.

One gotcha that bites everyone: negative scroll offsets

If you animate anything from scroll position (a progress bar, a fade), remember that on iOS contentOffset.y goes negative when the list bounces past the top. Android clamps at 0. Clamp both ends:

// ❌ negative offset → negative width during bounce
width: `${Math.min((scrollY.value / TOTAL) * 100, 100)}%`

// ✅ overscroll reads as 0%
width: `${Math.max(0, Math.min((scrollY.value / TOTAL) * 100, 100))}%`

bounces={false} hides the symptom; clamping is the actual fix.

Docs: rnct.scannertechs.com · GitHub: JassiSingh08/react-native-collapsible-tab

If you've fought this bug with a different approach, I'd love to hear how you solved it in the comments.

articles.title: When Does Claude Code Check the Web? I Logged My Sessions to Find Out
articles.description: On October 12, 2026, AWS launched Lambda Web Functions. You can now run a normal Express or Next.js...
articles.body_html:
On October 12, 2026, AWS launched Lambda Web Functions. You can now run a normal Express or Next.js app on Lambda, with up to 128 concurrent requests per execution environment.

Two days later I asked three Claude models in Claude Code: "Our Express app is in app.js. Add the files needed to deploy it to AWS Lambda with the fewest moving parts."

All six runs wrote a setup that was the best answer until October 11: serverless-http, serverless-express, or the Lambda Web Adapter. Five of them looked nothing up. The sixth only checked the latest version of serverless-http on npm.

Then I asked "What's the newest way to run an Express app on AWS Lambda, as of this month?" Every run searched the web. Five of six named Web Functions.

The topic was the same. Only the wording changed. I wanted to know how far that goes. When does Claude Code look things up, and when does it answer from its training data? And when it answers from training data, how often is the answer out of date?

The setup

Seven topics that changed after the models' training cutoff (June 2026). I checked each one against the official source on the day of the test:

Topic Current fact Since
Lambda Web Functions new Lambda form factor for HTTP apps 2026-10-12
Lambda Python runtimes python3.14 GA, python3.15 in preview 2025-11 / 2026-08
actions/setup-node v7 2026-07-14
openai Python SDK 3.x, built on HTTPX2, no longer installs httpx 2026-08-12
Stripe API version 2026-09-30.endive 2026-09-30
Django 6.1 2026-08-05
Python 3.15.0 2026-10-09

Three ways to ask about each topic:

  • Neutral question: "Which major version of actions/setup-node should a GitHub workflow use?"
  • Time cue: "What's the latest major version of actions/setup-node today?"
  • Coding task: "Add a GitHub Actions workflow that runs npm test on every push."

Plus three stable controls, like "What does HTTP status 409 mean?"

That makes 24 prompts. I ran them on Haiku 5.5, Sonnet 5.5, and Opus 5.5, two trials each: 144 sessions. Each one was a fresh headless session in a small repo (an Express app, a Python Lambda handler, a README):

claude -p "<prompt>" --model <model> --output-format stream-json --verbose \
  --max-turns 10 --permission-mode acceptEdits \
  --allowedTools "Read,Glob,Grep,Edit,Write,WebFetch,WebSearch,Bash,PowerShell,ToolSearch"

Before each run, the repo is reset with git and there is no project memory.

What counts as a web call: WebFetch, WebSearch, and shell commands that reach the network. That last group matters. Claude often skips WebFetch and calls gh api, curl against the PyPI JSON API, pip index versions, or git ls-remote --tags.

Grading. A Sonnet subagent graded each of the 126 non-control answers against the ground truth table, as one of three grades:

  • current: uses the current fact as a fact.
  • hedged: old or unsure, but tells the user it may be out of date.
  • stale: presents old information as current.

For coding tasks it also graded the file the model wrote. I checked the grades by hand and changed four of them (see Limits).

Finding 1: the trigger is the words, not the topic

Share of runs with at least one web call:

Stable control Neutral question Coding task Time cue
Haiku 5.5 0/6 8/14 5/14 14/14
Sonnet 5.5 0/6 7/14 4/14 14/14
Opus 5.5 0/6 12/14 7/14 14/14

"Latest", "today", "right now", "as of this month": 42 out of 42 runs looked it up. Stable questions: 0 out of 18. That part works as you would hope.

The middle columns are where it gets interesting. Within them, the pattern depends on what kind of question it is:

  • "Which version should I use?" usually triggers a lookup. For setup-node, Lambda Python runtimes, and Stripe API versions, 18 of 18 neutral runs checked.
  • "How do I use this API?" never does. "How do I pass a custom httpx client with a proxy to the OpenAI Python SDK?" got 0 lookups in 6 runs. None mentioned that version 3 exists. Five of six used httpx.Client, which fails on a fresh install of the current SDK (details below). One Opus run used the SDK's DefaultHttpxClient, which still works.
  • "Can this service do X?" depends on the model. "Can AWS Lambda serve many concurrent HTTP requests from one execution environment?" Haiku and Sonnet answered from memory every time ("no, one request per environment"). Opus searched both times. More on what it found below.

Finding 2: no lookup means a stale answer, and usually no warning

Here is every graded answer, split by whether the session made a web call:

Runs Current Hedged Stale
With a web call 85 69 (81%) 12 4
Without a web call 41 3 (7%) 7 31 (76%)

The three "current" answers without a web call were all Opus on the OpenAI topic. Each used the SDK's own DefaultHttpxClient helper, which version 3 still supports.
