In the two coding runs, Opus also ran the code against the installed package, which happened to be the current version. None of the three knew that version 3 exists. The code worked because the SDK kept an old name. Apart from that one case, no answer from training data alone was current.

That is expected for facts that changed after the cutoff. What I didn't expect was how rarely the models said so. Of the 35 stale answers, 28 gave no warning at all. The other 7 had some caveat, but often a narrow or generic one. For example, one answer warned about checking the Lambda Web Adapter layer version, but it didn't know Web Functions existed.

When Sonnet did hedge, the hedges were good ones: "Django 6.1 if it is out, I'm not sure it has shipped", "I answered from memory and did not check". When it hedged, it meant it.

Finding 3: coding tasks are the blind spot

Here is what ended up in the files for the coding tasks that did not mention "newest":

Task Web lookups What was written (6 runs) Current
GitHub workflow running npm test 0/6 setup-node@v4 (Haiku, Sonnet), @v5 (Opus) v7
SAM template for a Python Lambda 0/6 python3.13 (5 runs), python3.12 (1 run) python3.14
OpenAI client through a proxy 0/6 import httpx + httpx.Client(proxy=...) (Haiku, Sonnet), DefaultHttpxClient (Opus) DefaultHttpx2Client
Express app on Lambda 1/6 serverless-http, serverless-express, Lambda Web Adapter Web Functions
Stripe client with a pinned API version 3/6 2026-09-30.endive (3), 2025-09-30.clover, 2025-03-31.basil, 2024-06-20 2026-09-30.endive

The Stripe row shows it best. Opus searched in both runs and pinned the current version. Haiku searched in one of two runs and got it right in that one. Sonnet never searched and pinned versions from 2025.

Two coding tasks did trigger lookups every time: "pin Django to the newest stable version" and "a Dockerfile on the newest stable Python". 12 out of 12. The word "newest" in the coding task was enough.

The OpenAI row needs a note, because "outdated" can mean "still works". I checked it in a clean virtual environment with only openai==3.31.0 installed. The Haiku and Sonnet code fails on its first line:

ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'httpx'

openai 3.x depends on httpx2 and no longer pulls in httpx. In an older environment that still has httpx, the same code runs. The Opus version uses the SDK's own DefaultHttpxClient, which 3.x keeps as an alias built on httpx2. That one works on a fresh install too.

Finding 4: the training data is older than the cutoff

These models have a June 2026 training cutoff. But look at what the coding tasks wrote:

  • Lambda added python3.14 on November 18, 2025, seven months before the cutoff. All six SAM templates used 3.13 or 3.12.
  • actions/setup-node v6 shipped in October 2025. Haiku and Sonnet wrote v4 (2023). Opus wrote v5 (September 2025).
  • Haiku pinned Stripe API version 2024-06-20.

So "the model knows things up to its cutoff" is too generous for coding defaults. My guess at the reason: when a model writes a version from memory, it writes the version it saw most in training. That is the version most existing code used, often a year or two behind the cutoff. The newest versions are thin in the training data, because little code used them yet.

The practical effect: checking whether something changed after the cutoff is not enough. A version pinned from memory can be stale even for things released well before it.

Finding 5: a lookup is not the same as a current answer

Four stale answers came after a web call. They show two different ways a search can fail.

The search asked about what the model already knew. On "Can AWS Lambda serve many concurrent HTTP requests from one execution environment?", Opus searched both times. Both times the query was:

AWS Lambda Managed Instances multi-concurrency execution environment

Lambda Managed Instances is a real feature from late 2025. Opus knew it from training, searched to confirm it, and got a good, sourced answer about Managed Instances. It never found Web Functions, launched two days earlier, which is the direct answer to the question. The search was built from the model's memory, so it could only confirm that memory.

The search index was behind. Python 3.15.0 came out on October 9. On October 14, Sonnet searched "latest stable Python release python.org downloads" and got cached snapshots of python.org listing 3.14.8 as the newest release and 3.15 as a pre-release. It wrote python:3.14-slim into the Dockerfile. In a different run, the query "latest stable Python release version October 2026" found 3.15. The search with the month in it worked. The one without it got old snapshots.

To be fair, Sonnet said it got the version from a web search. And when asked the plain question ("What is the newest stable Python release today?"), it got the same stale snapshots. Both times it said the search results disagreed, and once it added that 3.15 "may have shipped since". It was honest about the gap. In the Dockerfile run, it still wrote the old version.

Finding 6: one line in CLAUDE.md fixes most of it

If the gap is that coding tasks don't trigger lookups, the obvious fix is to tell the model to look things up. I added this CLAUDE.md to the repo and reran the seven coding tasks, 3 models x 2 trials:

Your training data may be out of date. Before you write any version number,
runtime identifier, GitHub Action version, API version, or SDK usage pattern
into a file, look up the current value (web, package registry, or official
docs). Prefer the newest stable option unless the repo pins something else.

Coding tasks with a web lookup went from 16 of 42 runs to 42 of 42. Answers graded current went from 15 of 42 to 33 of 42.

Per task, files with the current value (6 runs each):

Task Without CLAUDE.md With CLAUDE.md
GitHub workflow (setup-node) 0/6 6/6 (@v7)
SAM template (Python runtime) 0/6 6/6 (python3.14)
Stripe client (API version) 3/6 6/6 (2026-09-30.endive)
OpenAI client through a proxy 2/6 work 4/6 (DefaultHttpx2Client), Haiku still wrote import httpx
Django requirements ("newest") 6/6 6/6
Dockerfile ("newest" Python) 5/6 5/6
Express app on Lambda 0/6 0/6 (Opus found Web Functions, then ran out of turns)

Version pins are fixed. The two tasks that already said "newest" didn't change, because they were already looking things up.

Two things the rule did not fully fix:

Haiku looked up the version, not the API. On the OpenAI task, Haiku checked the latest version on PyPI both times. It then wrote the same import httpx code as before. It treated "look up" as "find the version number", not "find out how the SDK is used now". Sonnet and Opus read the SDK README and wrote DefaultHttpx2Client.

The approach changed only for the models that read past the version number. Haiku and Sonnet used the rule to look up versions for the approach they had already chosen from memory: the latest serverless-http on npm, the latest Lambda Web Adapter layer, the latest Node runtime. One Sonnet run also opened the AWS page on Web Functions runtimes. It then named Web Functions as an alternative and explained why it didn't use them: app.js would need a small change, and it wasn't sure SAM supports them yet. That's a reasonable call. The other Haiku and Sonnet runs never mentioned Web Functions.

Opus went further. In both runs, the Lambda runtimes page led it to Web Functions. It then read the Web Functions runtimes page, the samples, the "create" guide, and the aws lambda-web deploy CLI reference. It was clearly heading for the new approach. Then both runs hit my 10-turn limit before writing a file. So I can't say what it would have written, only that the rule made it find the feature that launched two days earlier.

The cost of the rule: across the 42 coding runs, the total went from $2.51 to $4.47 (+78%), and Sonnet's average time went from 10 to 18 seconds. For setup work that pins versions, that's cheap. For every small edit, you may not want it.

The models compared

Avg web calls per run Coding tasks graded current Cost for 48 runs
Haiku 5.5 1.08 4/14 $0.57
Sonnet 5.5 0.81 3/14 $2.02
Opus 5.5 1.33 8/14 $5.68

Opus looks things up the most, mostly on neutral questions (12 of 14 against 7 or 8 for the others), and it is the only one that searched on the Stripe coding task both times. Haiku searched more than Sonnet. Sonnet was the most likely to answer from memory, and also the most likely to say so.

Costs are the total_cost_usd Claude Code reports per session. The whole experiment cost about $8.30 for the 144 main runs, plus $4.50 for the 42 CLAUDE.md runs.

Limits

  • Two trials per model. The patterns were very stable across trials, but rare behavior won't show up.
  • Seven topics. All are developer tooling with a version number or a launch date. I didn't test topics where "what changed" is fuzzier.
  • Headless sessions with acceptEdits. An interactive session may behave a bit differently.
  • One grader, a Sonnet subagent, with my spot checks. I changed four grades in two cases. One rewarded a generic "AWS may have changed" footer. In the other three, old-style OpenAI code turned out to still work on the new SDK.
  • A 10-turn cap. Both Opus runs of the Express task with the CLAUDE.md rule hit it while reading the Web Functions docs, so they wrote no files. With a higher cap, that row would probably look better for Opus.
  • The test date was close to the launches on purpose. Lambda Web Functions were two days old. That is the hardest case, and the most realistic one for "what changed last week".

What I take from this

Time words are the trigger. "Latest", "newest", "current", "today": with them, all three models looked things up in every run. Without them, the model mostly answers from memory.

Coding tasks don't trigger lookups. "Write a workflow", "write a SAM template", "write a Stripe client" all pin a version, and the model picks it from memory. Most of the stale values in this test were written into files, not stated in answers.

"How do I use this API?" is the hardest case. It doesn't sound time-sensitive, so no model checked. But SDKs change their APIs, and the answer is the old API with no warning.

Read the version pins in every diff. Actions versions, runtime identifiers, API version strings, base image tags. These are the lines most likely to come from old training data, and the easiest to check.

Put the rule in CLAUDE.md. One paragraph took version pins in coding tasks from 0 of 6 to 6 of 6 for setup-node and the Lambda runtime. It costs extra lookups on every coding task. It fixes versions reliably. It changes the approach only when the model reads beyond the version number, which Opus did and Haiku did not.

When you need the newest thing, say "newest", and name the month if it's recent. "Newest stable Python" triggered a lookup every time. "October 2026" in the query got past stale search snapshots. And if you know a feature launched last week, name it. A search built from the model's memory can only confirm that memory.

articles.title: Doom Ran Inside TypeScript's Type Checker. Here's How Types Execute Code
articles.description: Doom's first frame took 12 days of type checking. The machinery: recursive conditional types, tuple-length math, and the limits tsc enforces.
articles.body_html:
• Book: The TypeScript Type System
  • Also by me: The TypeScript Library — the 5-book collection
  • My project: Hermes IDE | GitHub — an IDE for developers who ship with Claude Code and other AI coding tools
  • Me: xgabriel.com | GitHub

The first frame of Doom took 12 days to render. None of the game's code ran as JavaScript. The TypeScript type checker evaluated it, at about 20 million type instantiations per second, until the frame came out the other end as a type.

That was February 2025. Dimitri Mitropoulos, founder of Michigan TypeScript, published a video showing Doom running on a WebAssembly virtual machine written entirely in TypeScript types. Simon Willison's write-up puts the scale at 177 TB of data, or about 3.5 trillion lines of type definitions. Socket's coverage adds that a typical TypeScript app might produce 200,000 to 500,000 type instantiations in total. Doom needed 20 million of them every second, for 12 days straight.

The stunt is absurd on purpose, but it runs on the same recursive conditional types, infer, and template literals you already use for route parsers and deep Partial helpers. You can build a small adder out of that machinery in a few lines, and the walls it hits are the ones Doom had to tear down.

What actually ran

Mitropoulos did not write Doom in types. He wrote a WebAssembly runtime in types, then fed it Doom compiled to WebAssembly. The runtime is public on GitHub and its README describes it as a WebAssembly runtime "implemented purely in TypeScript types": you give it a program, the type checker evaluates it, and the result is a type.

According to Socket, the runtime implements the 116 WebAssembly instructions Doom needs, and the type checker executed about 18 million instructions, one at a time, to draw the first frame. To do it, the VM simulates RAM, a call stack, memory pointers, and an execution context, along with a type-level garbage collector and an L1 cache. Numbers live as binary two's complement digits inside string literal types.

The same article reports that the project needed up to 100 GB of memory, and that the first estimate for one frame was 1.25 petabytes of types over three months, before optimizations cut it to 177 TB in 12 days.


The type checker as a machine: types go in, a type comes out.

Conditional types are a loop with an exit

Every type-level program is built from one primitive: a conditional type that refers to itself.

type Last<T extends unknown[]> =
  T extends [...unknown[], infer L] ? L : never;

type TrimLeft<S extends string> =
  S extends ` ${infer Rest}` ? TrimLeft<Rest> : S;

type A = Last<[1, 2, 3]>;      // 3
type B = TrimLeft<"   hi">;   // "hi"

T extends X ? Yes : No is your if. infer is pattern matching that binds a variable. Referring to the alias inside its own branch is recursion. That is enough to compute anything a machine can, given unlimited time and memory, and tsc gives you neither.

TrimLeft is the example the TypeScript 4.5 release notes use, and it comes with a warning: before 4.5, a string with 50 leading spaces was enough to trigger "Type instantiation is excessively deep and possibly infinite."

Counting with tuple lengths

Types have no +. They do have tuples, and a tuple's length is a number literal type. So you count by building tuples.

type BuildTuple<
  N extends number,
  T extends unknown[] = [],
> = T["length"] extends N ? T : BuildTuple<N, [...T, unknown]>;

type Add<A extends number, B extends number> =
  [...BuildTuple<A>, ...BuildTuple<B>]["length"];

type Five = Add<2, 3>; // 5

BuildTuple<3> keeps appending unknown until the tuple's length equals 3. Add spreads two of those tuples into one and reads the length back out. Subtraction is the same trick in reverse: match [...BuildTuple<B>, ...infer Rest] and take the length of Rest.

The Doom runtime uses this exact move at its core. Its add.ts turns each binary digit into a tuple of zero or one element, spreads the two digits plus the carry into a single tuple, and reads the length (0 to 3) to decide the output digit and the next carry. Tuple length is the adder.

The three walls: 100 deep, 1,000 long, 5 million total

Now try Add<1500, 1>. It should fail, and the way it fails tells you which limit you hit.

tsc enforces three separate limits. Each one exists so a bad type cannot hang your editor:

  1. Instantiation depth: 100. Nested instantiations, where evaluating one type requires evaluating another inside it, stop at a depth of 100. PR #45711 set this in TypeScript 4.5. The old value was 50; an earlier change had raised it to 500, and users hit stack overflows.
  2. Tail-recursive iterations: 1,000. The same PR made tsc evaluate a conditional type whose branch is another conditional type in a loop instead of on the call stack. That loop gives up after 1,000 iterations.
  3. Instantiation count: 5 million. A running total of instantiations per checked expression or statement. Herrington Darkholme's walk through the checker source quotes the check as instantiationDepth === 100 || instantiationCount >= 5000000, alongside the tailCount === 1000 check for the loop.

BuildTuple is written in tail position: when it recurses, it returns the recursive result directly and does nothing else with it. That puts it in the 1,000-iteration loop instead of the 100-deep stack. Add<600, 700> should resolve to 1300, because each BuildTuple call stays under 1,000 iterations even though the final tuple is longer. Add<1500, 1> asks one BuildTuple for 1,500 iterations and runs into the cap.

Now break the tail position on purpose:

type Count<
  N extends number,
  T extends unknown[] = [],
> = T["length"] extends N
  ? []
  : [unknown, ...Count<N, [...T, unknown]>];

Count<N> also produces a tuple of length N, but it wraps the recursive call in a spread, so each step has to wait for the next one to finish. That is the non-tail shape the 4.5 release notes say won't be optimized. It runs against the depth limit instead of the iteration limit, and it gives up far sooner than BuildTuple does. The fix is the one the release notes give for their GetChars example: move the work into an accumulator parameter so the recursive call is the whole branch.

I haven't run these snippets for this post. Paste them into the TypeScript Playground and hover the aliases to see where your version of the compiler draws the line.


Three different limits stop three different kinds of recursion.

Doom does not fit under any of these walls. Socket reports that Mitropoulos temporarily patched the compiler during development to remove the safeguards: the type-instantiation depth limit, the recursion limits, the stack depth limit when comparing types, and the maximum size of unions and tuples, which he set to infinity. You will not get that build from npm. The Go-based compiler behind TypeScript 7 keeps these limits too. When someone asked in September 2026 whether they would be revisited for the new compiler, a maintainer answered: "We have no plans to change these limits."

Arithmetic on string literals

Tuple counting does not scale to 32-bit numbers. You cannot build a tuple of four billion elements. So the Doom runtime stores each number as a string of bits and does arithmetic one character at a time, like the adder circuit in a CPU.

Here is a small version. Bits are little-endian, least significant first, so the carry flows in the same direction tsc reads the string:

type Sum<A extends string, B extends string, C extends string> =
  `${A}${B}${C}` extends "000" ? ["0", "0"]
  : `${A}${B}${C}` extends "001" | "010" | "100" ? ["1", "0"]
  : `${A}${B}${C}` extends "011" | "101" | "110" ? ["0", "1"]
  : ["1", "1"];

type AddBits<
  A extends string,
  B extends string,
  C extends string = "0",
  Out extends string = "",
> = A extends `${infer a}${infer RestA}`
  ? B extends `${infer b}${infer RestB}`
    ? Sum<a, b, C> extends [
        infer D extends string,
        infer K extends string,
      ]
      ? AddBits<RestA, RestB, K, `${Out}${D}`>
      : never
    : never
  : C extends "1" ? `${Out}1` : Out;

// 3 + 1: "11" + "10" little-endian is "001", which is 4
type Four = AddBits<"11", "10">;

Sum is a one-bit full adder written as a lookup: three input bits, one output digit, one carry. AddBits peels the first character off each input with infer, adds them, appends the digit to Out, and recurses with the new carry. The recursive call sits at the end of a chain of conditional branches, so it is the shape PR #45711 evaluates in a loop. A 32-bit add takes about a hundred loop steps (three conditionals per bit), still well inside 1,000. The inputs must have the same length; the real runtime handles uneven inputs and pads to fixed widths.

The little-endian order matters. Template literal patterns match from the left, and ${infer a}${infer Rest} grabs the first character cheaply. Taking the last character means walking the whole string. Socket notes that because TypeScript only iterates strings from the left, Mitropoulos wrote all the binary algorithms in reverse. His add.ts reverses both inputs, adds, and reverses the result back, and a comment in the file calls that reversal a major recursion bottleneck.

Multiply, divide, and shift can follow the same pattern: a per-bit table plus a tail-recursive walk. Stack 116 of those instructions on a state machine that tracks memory and a program counter, and you have a CPU that runs in the checker.

What this means for the types you ship

You will never put Doom in your codebase. You will write a route parser, a typed SQL builder, a deep Paths<T> helper, or a schema-to-type mapper, and those run on the same machinery with the same three walls.

Keep recursion in tail position. If a recursive call is wrapped in a union, a spread, or an object, add an accumulator parameter and return the call bare. That moves your type from the 100-deep wall to the 1,000-iteration one.

Know which wall you hit. "Excessively deep and possibly infinite" is TS2589, and it can come from depth, from the iteration cap, or from the 5 million total. The fix differs: depth wants tail calls, the iteration cap wants shorter inputs or chunking, and the total wants fewer distributive unions in the hot path.

Next time TS2589 shows up in a helper you wrote, run tsc --extendedDiagnostics before you blame the IDE. It prints where the compiler spends its time and how many types it creates, which is your first clue to which of the three counters you blew.

If this was useful

Recursive conditional types, infer, template literal parsing, and the accumulator pattern that keeps you under the recursion limits are the core of The TypeScript Type System, book 2 in The TypeScript Library. If the AddBits walk made sense but you would not trust yourself to write the next one, that book takes you from generics to DSL-level types one step at a time.

The TypeScript Library — the 5-book collection. Books 1 and 2 are the core path; 3 and 4 substitute for 1 and 2 if you come from the JVM or PHP; book 5 is for anyone shipping TS at work.

  1. TypeScript Essentials — types, narrowing, modules, async, daily-driver tooling across Node, Bun, Deno, and the browser.
  2. The TypeScript Type System — generics, mapped/conditional types, infer, template literals, branded types.
  3. Kotlin and Java to TypeScript — variance, null safety, sealed classes to unions, coroutines to async/await.
  4. PHP to TypeScript — the sync-to-async shift, generics, discriminated unions for PHP 8+ developers.
  5. TypeScript in Production — tsconfig, build tools, monorepos, library authoring, dual ESM/CJS, JSR.

All five books ship in ebook, paperback, and hardcover.

articles.body_html:
A sitemap points to one URL.

The page declares another as canonical.

Internal links keep reinforcing a third version.

You can change the SEO plugin settings, but that is not really the problem. The system itself has no consistent answer to a basic question:

Which URL is the source of truth?

A surprising number of Technical SEO problems look like this. They surface in Search Console, indexing reports, or search performance, while the actual failure sits deeper in the application: routing, HTTP behavior, rendering, internal links, templates, caching, or deployment.

That is why Technical SEO is more useful when treated as an engineering concern rather than a collection of search-related settings.

For a page to compete in Google Search, several things have to work before content quality can even matter. The URL needs to be discoverable. Googlebot needs to be able to crawl it. The server has to return a usable response. Critical content has to survive the rendering path. Indexing signals should agree about which URL represents the page.

Google describes Search in terms of Crawling, Indexing, and Serving. For debugging, it is useful to treat Rendering as a separate failure domain—not because Google defines a different four-stage model, but because rendering failures are operationally different from crawl or indexation failures.

That distinction changes how you debug.

If a page “isn't in Google,” changing meta tags is not a useful first reaction.

First determine what actually failed.

Technical SEO Is a System Consistency Problem

A practical definition of Technical SEO for developers is this:

The engineering decisions that allow search engines to discover, process, and understand the correct content under the correct URL with as little ambiguity as possible.

That goes well beyond title tags and meta descriptions.

URL architecture, HTTP status codes, redirects, server-side and client-side rendering, internal links, JavaScript, pagination, faceted navigation, server response time, structured data, caching, and deployment can all affect what a crawler eventually sees and how a search engine interprets it.

Google's technical requirements for Search establish a few baseline conditions. In simplified form:

  • Googlebot must not be blocked from accessing the page.
  • The page must return a successful HTTP response.
  • The page must contain indexable content.

These are entry conditions, not ranking formulas.

The more interesting failures start when different parts of the platform disagree.

A sitemap says one thing. Routing says another. The template generates a different canonical. Internal links point somewhere else.

Each component may appear correct when inspected in isolation.

Together, they create ambiguity.

This is also where the boundary between SEO and engineering becomes more concrete.

An SEO requirement might say:

“Filter pages need to be controlled.”

That is not implementation-ready.

Engineering still needs answers to questions such as:

  • Which filter combinations should be indexable?
  • Which URLs should be crawlable?
  • Which URL is canonical for each state?
  • How should pagination behave?
  • What happens to URL parameters?
  • Which combinations redirect?
  • How does caching affect the returned HTML?

The requirement becomes useful only when it turns into predictable, testable system behavior.

Start by Identifying the Failure Domain

When someone reports that a page “isn't in Google,” there are several very different possibilities hiding behind that sentence.

The URL may never have been discovered.

It may have been discovered but not successfully crawled.

The response may be valid, but critical content may fail during rendering.

The page may render correctly but remain outside the index.

Or it may already be indexed and simply not be served for the query being tested.

Those are not variations of the same bug.

They belong to different layers.

Domain Engineering question Common failures Useful evidence
Discovery / Crawling Can the crawler discover and retrieve the URL? Orphan pages, blocked crawling, broken links, redirect chains, server failures Server logs, Crawl Stats, internal crawler
Rendering Does the expected content exist after JavaScript runs? Empty app shell, runtime errors, failed APIs, interaction-dependent lazy loading Raw HTML, rendered DOM, URL Inspection, DevTools
Indexing Which URL and content version should enter the index? noindex, canonical conflicts, duplication, low-value generated pages URL Inspection, Page Indexing reports, canonical and sitemap audit
Serving / Ranking Is the indexed page relevant and competitive for the query? Intent mismatch, weak relevance, content quality issues Search Performance, SERP analysis, content evaluation

Google's own documentation separates crawling, indexing, and serving. The extra rendering layer here is a debugging convenience.

It helps prevent one of the most expensive habits in Technical SEO: changing something simply because it is easy to change.

A canonical tag is easy to edit.

A cache plugin is easy to switch.

A metadata field is easy to rewrite.

None of those actions are useful if the failure actually starts in routing, server responses, JavaScript execution, or URL discovery.

Crawlability Starts With Architecture, Not robots.txt

Googlebot discovers URLs through links, sitemaps, redirects, and other crawl paths.

For internal navigation, important URLs should be represented by real links—normally an <a> element with a valid href.

This matters particularly in JavaScript applications. An interface element may look exactly like a link to a user while being implemented entirely through a click handler.

Visually, there is little difference.

Architecturally, there may be.

Google covers JavaScript-generated links and other related behavior in its JavaScript SEO guidance.

Crawlability also extends well beyond robots.txt.

A crawl problem can begin with:

  • Excessive click depth
  • Orphan pages
  • Redirect loops
  • Long redirect chains
  • Incorrect HTTP status codes
  • Slow or unstable endpoints
  • Unbounded URL parameters
  • Poorly designed faceted navigation

Large websites add another constraint: crawl resources are finite.

Google's crawl budget documentation is mainly relevant to large sites, rapidly changing sites, or platforms with large URL spaces.

For a small site, crawl budget itself may not deserve much attention.

But bad URL architecture still does.

An e-commerce platform is a good example. Sorting, filters, pagination, search parameters, and category combinations can create a huge number of URLs from a relatively small catalogue.

The expensive mistake is to solve this after launch.

By then, thousands or millions of URL combinations may already exist in the crawl space.

The better place to make that decision is in the URL model.

robots.txt, noindex, and Canonical Solve Different Problems

These three controls often appear together in audits, but they do not do the same job.

robots.txt controls whether a crawler is allowed to crawl a URL.

noindex tells a search engine not to index a page or show it in search results.

rel="canonical" indicates a preferred URL among duplicate or highly similar URLs.

The distinction matters.

Google's robots meta documentation explains an important constraint around noindex: the crawler generally needs access to the page in order to observe the directive.

Blocking a URL in robots.txt and then expecting Googlebot to read the noindex directive from that same URL is therefore a contradictory design.

Canonicalization is a different problem again.

A canonical is not a deletion instruction.

Google's canonicalization guidance treats it as a signal for choosing a representative URL among duplicates or near-duplicates.

A useful mental model is:

  • robots.txt → Should this URL be crawled?
  • noindex → Should this page enter the index?
  • rel="canonical" → Which URL should represent this content cluster?

When these tools are mixed without a clear model, debugging becomes much harder because you no longer know which layer the implementation is trying to control.

Rendering: “Google Can Run JavaScript” Is the Wrong Question

Google can render JavaScript.

That fact is useful, but it is not a rendering strategy.

As more of a page depends on JavaScript, APIs, asynchronous data, client-side routing, authentication state, and third-party resources, the path between the initial HTTP response and the final content gains more moving parts.

Each one can fail.

Typical dependencies include:

  • API requests
  • JavaScript bundles
  • Runtime execution
  • Authentication
  • Network requests
  • Lazy loading
  • Client-side state
  • Third-party scripts

Google documents the relationship between crawling, rendering, and indexing for JavaScript sites in JavaScript SEO Basics.

The useful engineering question is not:

“Can Google run this JavaScript?”

It is:

“Should indexing this content depend on all of these things working correctly?”

That is a different standard.

For important content pages, server-side rendering, static generation, or server-generated HTML can reduce the number of runtime dependencies required before the core content becomes available.

That does not make client-side rendering wrong.

CSR may be entirely appropriate for an application.

The choice should come from the actual constraints of the system: latency, personalization, caching, interactivity, SEO requirements, infrastructure, and maintenance cost.

Not ideology.

Debug Rendering From Evidence

For a problematic JavaScript URL, start with three versions of the page:

  1. The raw HTML returned by the server
  2. The DOM after the browser executes JavaScript
  3. The rendered output visible through Google's inspection tooling

Then compare them.

Is the title present in all three?

The main content?

Internal links?

Canonical?

Structured data?

Status-dependent content?

This usually tells you more than changing a caching option and running the test again.

Indexing Is Where Inconsistent Signals Become Expensive

A crawler successfully retrieving a URL does not mean that URL will become the indexed representative of the content.

The search engine still has decisions to make.

Is the page duplicated elsewhere?

Which version is canonical?

Does the page contain enough unique and useful content?

Do internal links reinforce the same URL?

Does the sitemap agree?

Do redirects agree?

Google documents canonical selection as part of the indexing process, and its duplicate URL guidance distinguishes stronger signals such as redirects and rel="canonical" from weaker signals such as sitemap inclusion.

This is where Technical SEO becomes a system-integration problem.

Ideally, all of these components should make the same decision:

  • Routing
  • Redirect rules
  • Canonical generation
  • Sitemap generation
  • Internal links

If routing normalizes one URL but templates output another, the system is inconsistent.

If the sitemap contains parameterized URLs that templates canonicalize elsewhere, the system is inconsistent.

If internal links continue pointing to redirected URLs, the system is inconsistent.

These are good candidates for automated tests.

Canonicalization does not need to remain a manual SEO audit forever.

For important templates and route families, integration tests can verify things like:

  • Final HTTP status
  • Redirect destination
  • Canonical URL
  • Sitemap inclusion
  • Internal-link target format

That moves Technical SEO closer to normal software quality assurance—which is where much of it belongs.

Structured Data Is Better Treated as a Data Contract

Google defines Structured Data as a standardized way to provide information about a page and classify its content.

For engineering purposes, another useful way to think about it is as a data contract.

Imagine a product page where:

  • The visible price comes from one service
  • Availability comes from another
  • Breadcrumbs are generated from routing
  • JSON-LD is assembled independently in the SEO layer

Nothing guarantees these values will remain aligned.

You may eventually show one price to the user and another in Structured Data.

Or the page says “out of stock” while JSON-LD still reports availability.

The problem is not that the schema markup is syntactically invalid.

The problem is that two representations of the same entity have drifted apart.

A healthier implementation keeps Structured Data:

  • Consistent with visible content
  • Close to the same source of truth
  • Testable at the template or domain-model level
  • Limited to types and properties the page genuinely supports

More markup is not automatically better SEO.

If the data model is weak, more markup simply creates another representation that can become wrong.

Core Web Vitals Are Symptoms Until You Find the Cause

Performance work has a similar failure mode.

Teams see a score and immediately start optimizing the score.

But the score is not the architecture.

Google's current Web Vitals guidance defines the Core Web Vitals around:

  • LCP — loading performance
  • INP — interaction responsiveness
  • CLS — visual stability

The “good” thresholds are:

  • LCP: ≤ 2.5 seconds
  • INP: ≤ 200 milliseconds
  • CLS: ≤ 0.1

The assessment is based on the 75th percentile of real-user experiences.

That last part matters.

A Lighthouse run is useful, but it is not your users.

Lab data is excellent for reproducing problems, profiling code, and identifying regressions. Field data tells you what actual users are experiencing.

The most useful optimization work begins after the metric is connected to a cause.

A poor LCP might start with slow TTFB.

Then a late-discovered hero image makes it worse.

Then render-blocking CSS adds more delay.

Then client-side data fetching delays the final content again.

The final symptom is “bad LCP.”

The fix may belong to infrastructure, HTML generation, resource priority, CSS architecture, or rendering strategy.

The same principle applies to INP.

A poor INP value may point to long tasks, expensive JavaScript execution, or a component tree doing too much work on interaction.

CLS may come from image dimensions, font loading, ad slots, injected banners, or late-rendered components.

Changing a minification option may move the number.

It may not fix the system.

Technical SEO Needs Observability

A Technical SEO problem discovered only after traffic drops was probably observable earlier.

Not necessarily through one dashboard, but through the system.

Depending on scale, useful monitoring signals can include:

  • Crawl failures
  • HTTP status-code distribution
  • Sitemap errors
  • Canonical changes
  • Indexation patterns
  • Template-level Core Web Vitals
  • Unexpected robots changes
  • noindex changes
  • Spikes in 404 or 5xx responses
  • Unexpected changes in rendered HTML

Release monitoring matters too.

A deployment that modifies routing, templates, navigation, rendering, headers, or caching can affect Search behavior without touching anything explicitly labelled “SEO.”

For sensitive releases, a small smoke-test suite against representative URLs is cheap insurance.

Check the response.

Check redirects.

Check canonical output.

Check critical HTML.

Check rendered content.

Check robots directives.

A five-minute automated test after deployment is much cheaper than discovering a template-wide indexing problem two weeks later.

Server Logs, Crawlers, and Search Console Tell Different Stories

One mistake in Technical SEO investigations is expecting one tool to answer every question.

It cannot.

Server Logs

Server logs tell you what actually reached the server.

If Googlebot requested a URL, the logs can show it.

They can also expose response codes, crawl frequency, wasted requests, and patterns that are invisible from the frontend.

Internal Crawlers

A crawler tells you what your architecture exposes.

It can reveal orphan-like behavior, click depth, redirect chains, inconsistent canonicals, broken links, and URL patterns generated by the site.

That describes your system.

It does not prove Google behaved the same way.

Google Search Console

Search Console provides Google's reported view of discovery, crawling, indexing, canonicalization, and search performance.

That makes it extremely useful.

It still answers a different set of questions from your own crawler and server logs.

The three sources are complementary:

Server logs → what was requested

Crawler → what the architecture exposes

Search Console → what Google reports about processing and Search

When they disagree, that disagreement is often the interesting part.

A Debugging Workflow That Starts With Classification

A repeatable investigation is more useful than a large SEO checklist.

For a Technical SEO issue, this sequence works well as a starting point.

1. Classify the Failure

Decide whether the problem belongs primarily to:

Crawl → Render → Index → Serve

Do not propose a fix before deciding which domain failed.

2. Inspect the URL Outside the Normal Browser Flow

Check:

  • DNS
  • TLS
  • HTTP status
  • Redirects
  • Headers
  • Raw HTML

Browsers hide a surprising amount of complexity.

3. Review Directives Together

Do not inspect a canonical in isolation.

Check the interaction between:

  • robots.txt
  • Meta Robots
  • X-Robots-Tag
  • Canonical
  • hreflang, where relevant
  • Sitemap inclusion

4. Compare Raw and Rendered Output

For JavaScript pages, compare the server HTML, browser DOM, and Google's rendered view.

Look specifically at content and signals that matter for indexing.

5. Check Discovery Paths

An important page should normally be reachable through meaningful internal links.

If the only way to find a URL is an internal search box, you have an architecture problem before you have an SEO problem.

6. Use Field Data Before Optimizing Performance Blindly

If real-user data exists, start there.

Then use lab tooling to reproduce the problem and identify the cause.

7. Turn the Fix Into a Regression Test

This is the step that often gets skipped.

If a canonical bug affected thousands of URLs, write a test.

If a routing change created redirect chains, test routing.

If a template accidentally emitted noindex, add a deployment check.

Otherwise, you have fixed an incident—not the class of failure that caused it.

Pre-Release Technical SEO Checks

Before launching a new template, feature, migration, or routing change, verify the things that are expensive to discover later.

  • New URLs return the intended HTTP status.
  • Redirects terminate where expected.
  • Redirect chains have not been introduced accidentally.
  • Important pages are reachable through real HTML links.
  • Important URLs are not orphaned.
  • robots.txt, Meta Robots, and X-Robots-Tag match the intended behavior.
  • Canonicals resolve to the correct preferred URLs.
  • Sitemaps reinforce those same URLs.
  • Internal links do not keep pointing at deprecated or redirected variants.
  • Critical content exists in rendered HTML.
  • Important content does not require unnecessary user interaction before it appears.
  • Structured Data agrees with visible content.
  • Images and fonts do not introduce avoidable layout shifts.
  • Performance-sensitive changes are tested before deployment.
  • Representative URLs receive a post-deploy smoke test.
  • Server logs and Field Data are reviewed after higher-risk releases where appropriate.

This list is not a substitute for an audit.

It is a release guardrail.

Technical SEO Is Part of System Quality

The strongest Technical SEO implementations are usually not the ones with the largest number of SEO-specific settings.

They are the ones where the platform behaves predictably.

URLs have clear ownership.

Redirects are intentional.

Internal links reinforce canonical routes.

Critical content has a reliable rendering path.

Structured Data reflects the same underlying entities users see.

Performance problems can be traced to causes.

Important changes are observable after deployment.

That is why Technical SEO for developers is ultimately a system quality problem.

Crawlability, indexability, rendering reliability, and performance should not be attached to a project at the end as a separate optimization phase.

They belong alongside other non-functional requirements such as accessibility, reliability, security, and performance.

And when a site's problems are spread across the codebase, routing, rendering layer, Search Console, and content architecture, the useful starting point is not a list of fifty recommendations.

It is identifying the failure domain.

Then fixing the system that produced it.

References

The platform-specific claims in this article are based primarily on official Google documentation:

  • Google Search Central — How Google Search Works
  • Google Search Central — Google Search Technical Requirements
  • Google Search Central — JavaScript SEO Basics
  • Google Search Central — Robots Meta Tag Specifications
  • Google Search Central — Canonicalization and Duplicate URLs
  • Google Search Central — Introduction to Structured Data
  • Google Crawling Infrastructure — Crawl Budget Management
  • web.dev — Web Vitals

The Crawl → Render → Index → Serve model used throughout this article is an engineering diagnostic framework. It should not be interpreted as Google's official four-stage Search model.
